query.original_query: working memory capacity limit LLM holding multiple facts simultaneously interference recall

sub_queries.semantic_query: capacity limits of working memory in large language models, interference when holding multiple facts simultaneously, recall degradation and attention head specialization
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the capacity limits of working memory in large language models by analyzing interference patterns when models are prompted to hold multiple factual associations simultaneously. Using causal tracing and activation patching, we localize knowledge recall to specific MLP layers and attention heads, finding that recall degradation correlates with competition for shared attention head resources. Our analysis reveals that as the number of concurrently maintained facts increases, attention heads exhibit reduced specialization, with overlapping activation patterns across distinct factual queries. We further observe that interference is most pronounced in middle-layer attention heads, where multiple facts compete for the same residual stream subspaces. Results show that models exhibit a sharp decline in recall accuracy beyond a threshold of three to four simultaneous facts, consistent with behavioral working memory constraints. Activation patching experiments confirm that degrading specific attention heads disproportionately affects multi-fact recall, while single-fact retrieval remains robust. These findings suggest that attention head specialization imposes a structural bottleneck on concurrent factual storage, with interference arising from superposition-like dynamics in the residual stream.

sub_queries.semantic_query: working memory capacity limits, interference effects in holding multiple items simultaneously, recall of information from short-term memory, chunking strategies
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated the role of proactive interference in limiting the simultaneous maintenance of multiple items in working memory. Participants performed a modified complex span task requiring recall of serially presented list items while engaging in a concurrent processing demand. We manipulated the semantic similarity between to-be-remembered items across trials to assess the buildup of interference. Recall accuracy declined as the number of similar items held concurrently increased, consistent with interference-based accounts of capacity limits. Critically, we examined whether instructed chunking strategies could mitigate these interference effects. Results indicated that while chunking improved overall recall performance, it did not fully eliminate the detrimental impact of proactive interference on the precision of individual item representations. Findings support the hypothesis that working memory capacity is constrained not solely by a fixed number of slots, but by the resolution of competition between similar memory traces during retrieval. These results align with resource-sharing models of short-term memory.

papers.title: Self-Attention Limits Working Memory Capacity of Transformer-Based Models
papers.research_question: Why do transformer-based models exhibit working memory capacity limits in N-back tasks? The paper hypothesizes that the self-attention mechanism is responsible.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the self-attention mechanism in transformers limits working memory capacity, as increased task difficulty (larger N) leads to higher entropy in attention scores and lower accuracy, analogous to human attention limits.
papers.conclusion: The self-attention mechanism in transformers is both essential for performing the N-back task and responsible for its working memory capacity limits, mirroring the role of selective attention in human cognition.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer model performance on N-back tasks declines as N increases, similar to human working memory limits.
During training, attention scores learn to focus on the N-back position, but this focus becomes less precise as N increases.
Accuracy at a given position is positively correlated with the attention score at the corresponding N-back position.
The total entropy of the attention score matrix increases with N, indicating greater dispersion of attention and lower accuracy.
Even models with more layers and heads show a slight decline in accuracy with increasing N, suggesting a fundamental limit.
papers.limitation: The study uses a simplified Transformer model without FFNs and layer normalization, limiting direct comparison to pre-trained LLMs.
future_direction: Explore a formal mathematical proof for capacity limits in complex intelligent systems.
Investigate how model architecture complexity and number of parameters affect task performance.
Study the impact of training data amount and hyperparameters on model behavior.
papers.abstract: Recent work on Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) has revealed striking limits in their working memory capacity, similar to what has been found in human behavioral studies. Specifically, these models' performance drops significantly on N-back tasks as N increases. However, there is still a lack of mechanistic interpretability as to why this phenomenon would arise. Inspired by the executive attention theory from behavioral sciences, we hypothesize that the self-attention mechanism within Transformer-based models might be responsible for their working memory capacity limits. To test this hypothesis, we train vanilla decoder-only transformers to perform N-back tasks and find that attention scores gradually aggregate to the N-back positions over training, suggesting that the model masters the task by learning a strategy to pay attention to the relationship between the current position and the N-back position. Critically, we find that the total entropy of the attention score matrix increases as N increases, suggesting that the dispersion of attention scores might be the cause of the capacity limit observed in N-back tasks. Our findings thus offer insights into the shared role of attention in both human and artificial intelligence. Moreover, the limitations of the self-attention mechanism revealed in the current study could inform future efforts to design more powerful model architectures with enhanced working memory capacity and cognitive capabilities.

papers.title: A Language Model with Limited Memory Capacity Captures Interference in Human Sentence Processing
papers.research_question: Can a neural language model with limited memory capacity capture similarity-based interference effects in human sentence processing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a cue-based retrieval recurrent neural network (CBR-RNN) with a single attention head, demonstrating that it can capture similarity-based interference effects in human sentence processing without hand-picked linguistic features.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that mechanistic explanations of processing difficulty rooted in memory retrieval constraints can emerge as a by-product of minimizing the surprisal of upcoming words.
papers.key_findings:
The CBR-RNN's attention mechanism tracks subject-verb dependencies over long distances and with intervening nouns.
The model captures both semantic and syntactic interference effects in agreement attraction experiments.
Surprisal estimates from the model predict human plausibility ratings for attraction effects.
Relative attention from the single head shows additive effects of semantic and agreement attraction in double violations.
GPT-2's attention heads exhibit complementary interference effects, highlighting challenges in aggregating multiple heads.
papers.limitation:
Limited to subject-verb dependencies, not other dependency types.
Assumptions about working memory differ from cue-based theories, e.g., items are timestep representations not syntactic constituents.
It is unclear if the model learns interpretable linguistic features like [+/-subject].
Training data is from Wikipedia, not developmentally plausible like child-directed speech.
future_direction: Evaluate on various dependency types like reflexive anaphora and filler-gap dependencies.
Incorporate syntactic attention masking or memory decay mechanisms.
Use causal representational probing to interpret learned features.
papers.abstract: Two of the central factors believed to underpin human sentence processing difficulty are expectations and retrieval from working memory. A recent attempt to create a unified cognitive model integrating these two factors relied on the parallels between the self-attention mechanism of transformer language models and cue-based retrieval theories of working memory in human sentence processing (Ryu and Lewis 2021). While Ryu and Lewis show that attention patterns in specialized attention heads of GPT-2 are consistent with similarity-based interference, a key prediction of cue-based retrieval models, their method requires identifying syntactically specialized attention heads, and makes the cognitively implausible assumption that hundreds of memory retrieval operations take place in parallel. In the present work, we develop a recurrent neural language model with a single self-attention head, which more closely parallels the memory system assumed by cognitive theories. We show that our model's single attention head captures semantic and syntactic interference effects observed in human experiments.

papers.title: Language Models Do Not Have Human-Like Working Memory
papers.research_question: Can large language models maintain and manipulate unexpressed internal representations (latent state persistence) analogous to human working memory?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs lack the ability to maintain persistent latent states (working memory), functioning instead as reactive post-hoc reasoners, which highlights a fundamental architectural divergence from human-like cognition.
papers.conclusion: Current LLMs lack the ability to persistently maintain and manipulate latent states, functioning as reactive post-hoc reasoners rather than proactive planners, which poses a bottleneck for autonomous agents and tasks requiring working memory.
papers.key_findings:
In the Number Guessing Game, LLMs fail to allocate probability mass to a singular hidden choice, violating the sum-of-probability identity.
In the Yes-No Game, as the number of questions increases, LLMs suffer from concept drift and inevitable self-contradictions due to lack of latent state persistence.
In Mathematical Mentalism, LLMs fail to track transformations on hidden variables, revealing a failure in variable binding and state evolution when the initial state is not explicitly present.
Scaling and long-reasoning traces (e.g., in o3-Mini or DeepSeek-R1) do not bridge the latent state persistence gap; the underlying latent persistence remains absent.
LLMs exhibit human-centric priors such as the 'Blue-Seven' phenomenon, indicating reliance on stochastic priors rather than committed internal states.
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable reasoning abilities, we demonstrate that they lack a fundamental aspect of human cognition: working memory. Human working memory is an active cognitive system that enables not only the temporary storage of information but also its processing and utilization, enabling coherent reasoning and decision-making. Without working memory, individuals may produce unrealistic responses, exhibit self-contradictions, and struggle with tasks that require mental reasoning. Existing evaluations using N-back or context-dependent tasks fall short as they allow LLMs to exploit external context rather than retaining the reasoning process in the latent space. We introduce three novel tasks: (1) Number Guessing, (2) Yes-No Deduction, and (3) Math Magic, designed to isolate internal representation from external context. Across seventeen frontier models spanning four major model families, we consistently observe irrational or contradictory behaviors, indicating LLMs' inability to retain and manipulate latent information. Our work establishes a new benchmark for evaluating working memory in LLMs and highlights this limitation as a key bottleneck for advancing reliable reasoning systems. Code and prompts for the experiments are available at https://github.com/penguinnnnn/LLM-Working-Memory.

papers.title: Summing Up the Facts: Additive Mechanisms Behind Factual Recall in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do transformer-based large language models (LLMs) store and retrieve factual knowledge? The paper investigates the mechanistic story behind factual recall, focusing on prompts of the form 'Fact: The Colosseum is in the country of ____.'
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that factual recall in LLMs is achieved through an additive combination of multiple independent mechanisms (subject heads, relation heads, mixed heads, MLPs), termed the 'additive motif', and extends direct logit attribution to attribute attention head outputs to individual source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall in LLMs is achieved through additive combination of multiple independent mechanisms, and this additive motif may be a general principle in how models compute.
papers.key_findings:
There are four distinct mechanisms (subject heads, relation heads, mixed heads, MLPs) that additively combine to produce factual recall.
Each mechanism independently contributes to the correct logit, and their sum results in constructive interference, even if individual mechanisms are insufficient alone.
The additive motif explains why models often produce incorrect attributes alongside correct ones.
Extending direct logit attribution to attribute head outputs to source tokens reveals mixed heads as two separate additive updates from subject and relation tokens.
The work highlights a limitation of narrow circuit analysis that ignores multiple sources of information in prompts.
papers.limitation:
The dataset is small and hand-written, which may limit generalizability.
The analysis is limited to a specific prompting format and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Understanding correlation and superposition in feature representations
Understanding MLP neurons in detail
Studying how different prompting setups affect factual recall mechanisms
papers.abstract: How do transformer-based large language models (LLMs) store and retrieve knowledge? We focus on the most basic form of this task -- factual recall, where the model is tasked with explicitly surfacing stored facts in prompts of form `Fact: The Colosseum is in the country of'. We find that the mechanistic story behind factual recall is more complex than previously thought. It comprises several distinct, independent, and qualitatively different mechanisms that additively combine, constructively interfering on the correct attribute. We term this generic phenomena the additive motif: models compute through summing up multiple independent contributions. Each mechanism's contribution may be insufficient alone, but summing results in constructive interfere on the correct answer. In addition, we extend the method of direct logit attribution to attribute an attention head's output to individual source tokens. We use this technique to unpack what we call `mixed heads' -- which are themselves a pair of two separate additive updates from different source tokens.

papers.title: Understanding Fact Recall in Language Models: Why Two-Stage Training Encourages Memorization but Mixed Training Teaches Knowledge
papers.research_question: Why does two-stage training encourage memorization while mixed training teaches knowledge, and how do shared parameters internally support fact recall in mixed training?
papers.core_contribution: Mixed training teaches knowledge by increasing the quantity and collective importance of shared parameters, which are concentrated in critical attention heads for fact recall. The paper introduces cross-task gradient trace to analyze these parameters.
papers.conclusion: Mixed training teaches knowledge by increasing the quantity and collective importance of shared parameters, which are concentrated in critical attention heads for fact recall. The cross-task gradient trace tool can be used to analyze such mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Mixed training yields more shared parameters (those influenced by both fact-storing and fact-recalling examples) than two-stage training.
Shared parameters are concentrated in critical attention heads and are key to enabling fact recall in mixed-trained models.
Ablating shared parameters leads to a larger performance drop in mixed-trained models compared to two-stage trained models.
Mixed training achieves more parameter-efficient fact recall, requiring fewer parameters to recover performance.
Shared parameters in mixed training are more centralized and functionally important for generalization.
future_direction: Explore whether similar mechanisms emerge in other cross-task settings.
papers.abstract: Fact recall, the ability of language models (LMs) to retrieve specific factual knowledge, remains a challenging task despite their impressive general capabilities. Common training strategies often struggle to promote robust recall behavior with two-stage training, which first trains a model with fact-storing examples (e.g., factual statements) and then with fact-recalling examples (question-answer pairs), tending to encourage rote memorization rather than generalizable fact retrieval. In contrast, mixed training, which jointly uses both types of examples, has been empirically shown to improve the ability to recall facts, but the underlying mechanisms are still poorly understood. In this work, we investigate how these training strategies affect how model parameters are shaped during training and how these differences relate to their ability to recall facts. We introduce cross-task gradient trace to identify shared parameters, those strongly influenced by both fact-storing and fact-recalling examples. Our analysis on synthetic fact recall datasets with the Llama-3.2B and Pythia-2.8B models reveals that mixed training encouraging a larger and more centralized set of shared parameters. These findings suggest that the emergence of parameters may play a key role in enabling LMs to generalize factual knowledge across task formulations.

papers.title: Interpreting Key Mechanisms of Factual Recall in Transformer-Based Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer-based language models perform factual recall, specifically how do they extract arguments from context and apply implicit functions through MLPs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a detailed mechanistic interpretation of factual recall in transformers, introducing a method to decompose MLP outputs and identifying a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer.
papers.conclusion: The paper outlines a pipeline for factual recall in transformers, proposes a novel analytic method for MLPs, and identifies a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism that can be mitigated to improve factual recall confidence.
papers.key_findings:
Task-specific attention heads extract topic tokens and pass them to subsequent MLPs.
MLPs act as activations that amplify or erase individual attention head outputs in the residual stream.
Deep MLPs apply implicit functions by adding a task-aware component that redirects the residual stream towards the correct answer.
A universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer suppresses correct predictions, which can be mitigated using the proposed interpretation.
These mechanisms are consistent across models (GPT-2, OPT, Llama-2), tasks (country-capital, product-developer), and few-shot settings.
papers.limitation:
The paper does not explore how the model constructs task semantics within its shallow layers.
The origins of the identified mechanisms (e.g., why MLPs redirect the residual stream) need further research.
The proposed analysis method for decomposing MLP outputs requires preliminary human reasoning and is not fully automated.
future_direction: Exploring how task semantics are constructed in shallow layers through collaborative circuit paths.
Investigating the origins of the mechanisms, such as why MLP outputs are structured as y-x.
Developing more automated interpretation techniques for MLPs.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we delve into several mechanisms employed by Transformer-based language models (LLMs) for factual recall tasks. We outline a pipeline consisting of three major steps: (1) Given a prompt ``The capital of France is,'' task-specific attention heads extract the topic token, such as ``France,'' from the context and pass it to subsequent MLPs. (2) As attention heads' outputs are aggregated with equal weight and added to the residual stream, the subsequent MLP acts as an ``activation,'' which either erases or amplifies the information originating from individual heads. As a result, the topic token ``France'' stands out in the residual stream. (3) A deep MLP takes ``France'' and generates a component that redirects the residual stream towards the direction of the correct answer, i.e., ``Paris.'' This procedure is akin to applying an implicit function such as ``get\_capital($X$),'' and the argument $X$ is the topic token information passed by attention heads. To achieve the above quantitative and qualitative analysis for MLPs, we proposed a novel analytic method aimed at decomposing the outputs of the MLP into components understandable by humans. Additionally, we observed a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer of models, which suppresses correct predictions. We mitigate this suppression by leveraging our interpretation to improve factual recall confidence. The above interpretations are evaluated across diverse tasks spanning various domains of factual knowledge, using various language models from the GPT-2 families, 1.3B OPT, up to 7B Llama-2, and in both zero- and few-shot setups.

papers.title: Does Time Have Its Place? Temporal Heads: Where Language Models Recall Time-specific Information
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how language models encode and recall time-specific information, focusing on whether there are specific attention heads dedicated to temporal knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers Temporal Heads, specific attention heads in language models that encode and recall time-specific knowledge, and shows that ablating them impairs temporal knowledge while leaving other capabilities intact.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Temporal Heads are crucial for temporal knowledge in LLMs, and targeting them can enable precise temporal updates without global retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Temporal Heads, such as a15.h0 and a18.h3 in Llama2, are identified across multiple models and are crucial for temporal knowledge recall.
Ablating Temporal Heads significantly reduces accuracy on temporal knowledge tasks but has minimal effect on time-invariant knowledge and general QA performance.
Temporal Heads are activated for both numerical (e.g., 'In 2004') and textual (e.g., 'In the year...') temporal conditions, indicating they encode a broad temporal dimension.
Temporal knowledge can be edited by adjusting the activations of these heads, enabling targeted updates.
Backup Temporal Heads exist that can compensate when primary heads are ablated, ensuring model robustness.
papers.limitation:
Analysis of unstructured temporal QAs was constrained due to lack of temporal dependencies in options.
EAP-IG does not support models with Grouped-Query Attention, limiting analysis of models like Llama-3.
future_direction: Future work should focus on broader application for enhancing temporal reasoning and time-aware model alignment.
papers.abstract: While the ability of language models to elicit facts has been widely investigated, how they handle temporally changing facts remains underexplored. We discover Temporal Heads, specific attention heads that primarily handle temporal knowledge, through circuit analysis. We confirm that these heads are present across multiple models, though their specific locations may vary, and their responses differ depending on the type of knowledge and its corresponding years. Disabling these heads degrades the model's ability to recall time-specific knowledge while maintaining its general capabilities without compromising time-invariant and question-answering performances. Moreover, the heads are activated not only numeric conditions ("In 2004") but also textual aliases ("In the year ..."), indicating that they encode a temporal dimension beyond simple numerical representation. Furthermore, we expand the potential of our findings by demonstrating how temporal knowledge can be edited by adjusting the values of these heads.

papers.title: Unveiling Factual Recall Behaviors of Large Language Models through Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How effectively do Large Language Models retrieve and utilize their internal factual knowledge for multi-hop reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs often fail to retrieve relevant factual knowledge during reasoning; enhancing factual recall improves reasoning performance, while Chain-of-Thought prompting helps by stimulating step-by-step reasoning and reducing shortcuts.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall is crucial for correct reasoning in LLMs; CoT stimulates recall and reduces shortcuts, and contextual conflicts can affect the retrieval process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not consistently retrieve pertinent factual knowledge for reasoning, with more than a third of reasoning errors stemming from deficiencies in retrieval.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting enhances factual recall by facilitating step-by-step reasoning, reducing the likelihood of shortcuts.
Manually enhancing the factual recall process improves reasoning performance, while suppressing it leads to notable degradation.
The presence of knowledge conflict in the context can enhance the retrieval of the corresponding fact during reasoning.
A considerable proportion of correctly answered questions under no CoT setting rely on shortcuts rather than full multi-hop reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability: Findings are based on specific LLMs and the TFRKN dataset; future research should extend to various models and datasets.
Theoretical Analysis: Empirical evidence is provided, but a deeper theoretical analysis is needed to fully comprehend the underlying reasons.
Practical Applications: The paper discusses theoretical aspects but does not delve into practical applications to enhance reasoning capabilities.
future_direction: Extend findings to verify generalizability across various models and datasets.
Conduct deeper theoretical analysis to understand the observed phenomena.
Explore how the findings can be applied in practical scenarios to enhance LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) actively recall or retrieve their internal repositories of factual knowledge when faced with reasoning tasks. Through an analysis of LLMs' internal factual recall at each reasoning step via Knowledge Neurons, we reveal that LLMs fail to harness the critical factual associations under certain circumstances. Instead, they tend to opt for alternative, shortcut-like pathways to answer reasoning questions. By manually manipulating the recall process of parametric knowledge in LLMs, we demonstrate that enhancing this recall process directly improves reasoning performance whereas suppressing it leads to notable degradation. Furthermore, we assess the effect of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a powerful technique for addressing complex reasoning tasks. Our findings indicate that CoT can intensify the recall of factual knowledge by encouraging LLMs to engage in orderly and reliable reasoning. Furthermore, we explored how contextual conflicts affect the retrieval of facts during the reasoning process to gain a comprehensive understanding of the factual recall behaviors of LLMs. Code and data will be available soon.

papers.title: Tracing Facts or just Copies? A critical investigation of the Competitions of Mechanisms in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in LLMs mediate the competition between factual recall from parametric memory and counterfactual information provided in context? Do they perform selective counterfactual suppression or general copy suppression, and are they domain-specific?
papers.core_contribution: Attention heads that promote factual output in LLMs operate via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, and their behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models showing more specialization.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms that attention heads mediate the competition between factual and counterfactual tokens via copy suppression, and their effects are domain-dependent, with implications for model interpretability and control.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads contribute to the competition between factual and counterfactual tokens, and modifying their strength affects the proportion of factual outputs.
The attention heads supporting factual tokens suppress copying in general, not just counterfactuals, as they also suppress factual tokens when facts are present in the prompt.
The effect of attention heads is sensitive to sentence structure and the presence of hints (factual token in the subject).
Attention heads exhibit domain specialization; their contribution varies by answer category (e.g., location, language, organization).
Larger models (Pythia-6.9B) show more specialized and category-sensitive patterns than smaller models (GPT-2).
papers.limitation: The experiments are limited to two models (GPT-2 and Pythia-6.9B) and do not cover more models or study attention modification of different heads on different domains in detail.
future_direction: Applying the methods to different models
Studying how each attention head interacts with different domains
Constructing new datasets on other domains (e.g., STEM) and applying similar techniques
papers.abstract: This paper presents a reproducibility study examining how Large Language Models (LLMs) manage competing factual and counterfactual information, focusing on the role of attention heads in this process. We attempt to reproduce and reconcile findings from three recent studies by Ortu et al., Yu, Merullo, and Pavlick and McDougall et al. that investigate the competition between model-learned facts and contradictory context information through Mechanistic Interpretability tools. Our study specifically examines the relationship between attention head strength and factual output ratios, evaluates competing hypotheses about attention heads' suppression mechanisms, and investigates the domain specificity of these attention patterns. Our findings suggest that attention heads promoting factual output do so via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, as strengthening them can also inhibit correct facts. Additionally, we show that attention head behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models exhibiting more specialized and category-sensitive patterns.

papers.title: Recognition, recall, and retention of few-shot memories in large language models
papers.research_question: What exactly can a language model remember about training examples that it sees only a few times? How long does that memory persist as the model is continued to be trained with new examples?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models can quickly memorize training examples with few exposures, but these memories are rapidly overwritten during continued training, though some residual memory persists. Recognition memory is more robust than recall and exceeds human performance.
papers.conclusion: Large language models are remarkably effective at fast memorization, but retention is a key challenge; improving retention might alleviate issues like hallucination, though perfect retention may not be desirable for generalization.
papers.key_findings:
A single exposure is sufficient for near-perfect recognition accuracy across various stimulus types, even for challenging distinctions like paraphrases.
Recall requires more exposures (typically 3) to achieve near-perfect performance, especially for natural language sentences.
Memory retention declines rapidly in the first few training updates with new data, then more gradually, with some memories persisting even after 100K updates.
Recognition memory is more robust to interference from new training than recall memory.
Memory for natural language sentences is superior to memory for structureless stimuli like random word sequences or random strings.
papers.limitation:
Need to evaluate bigger, more capable models beyond the 13B parameter models studied.
Limited experimental probes of memory, relying only on recognition tests and conditional recall with greedy decoding, which may be too stringent.
future_direction: Investigate whether ideas from continual learning can improve memory retention in neural networks.
Use more fine-grained measures of memory, such as sampling at different temperatures instead of greedy decoding.
Explore how instruction tuning affects memory properties of language models.
papers.abstract: The training of modern large language models (LLMs) takes place in a regime where most training examples are seen only a few times by the model during the course of training. What does a model remember about such examples seen only a few times during training and how long does that memory persist in the face of continuous training with new examples? Here, we investigate these questions through simple recognition, recall, and retention experiments with LLMs. In recognition experiments, we ask if the model can distinguish the seen example from a novel example; in recall experiments, we ask if the model can correctly recall the seen example when cued by a part of it; and in retention experiments, we periodically probe the model's memory for the original examples as the model is trained continuously with new examples. We find that a single exposure is generally sufficient for a model to achieve near perfect accuracy even in very challenging recognition experiments. We estimate that the recognition performance of even small language models easily exceeds human recognition performance reported in similar experiments with humans (Shepard, 1967). Achieving near perfect recall takes more exposures, but most models can do it in just 3 exposures. The flip side of this remarkable capacity for fast learning is that precise memories are quickly overwritten: recall performance for the original examples drops steeply over the first 10 training updates with new examples, followed by a more gradual decline. Even after 100K updates, however, some of the original examples are still recalled near perfectly. A qualitatively similar retention pattern has been observed in human long-term memory retention studies before (Bahrick, 1984). Finally, recognition is much more robust to interference than recall and memory for natural language sentences is generally superior to memory for stimuli without structure.

papers.title: Aspects of human memory and Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do Large Language Models exhibit human-like memory properties such as primacy and recency effects, and are these properties due to architectural biases or learned from training data?
papers.core_contribution: Large Language Models exhibit human-like memory properties such as primacy and recency effects, and these properties are likely learned from the statistical patterns in training data rather than being inherent to the transformer architecture.
papers.conclusion: The human-like memory properties observed in Large Language Models are likely learned from statistical patterns in human-generated text, suggesting that human memory characteristics influence the structure of narratives.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit primacy and recency effects in memory recall.
Adding elaborations to facts improves recall accuracy.
Forgetting in LLMs occurs primarily through interference rather than memory decay.
Repetitions improve recall, with spaced repetitions being more effective than immediate ones.
LLMs show a 'memory formation time' where recall improves with initial distance from the presented facts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are huge artificial neural networks which primarily serve to generate text, but also provide a very sophisticated probabilistic model of language use. Since generating a semantically consistent text requires a form of effective memory, we investigate the memory properties of LLMs and find surprising similarities with key characteristics of human memory. We argue that the human-like memory properties of the Large Language Model do not follow automatically from the LLM architecture but are rather learned from the statistics of the training textual data. These results strongly suggest that the biological features of human memory leave an imprint on the way that we structure our textual narratives.

papers.title: Flexible Working Memory Through Selective Gating and Attentional Tagging
papers.research_question: How can cognitive control over working memory content be acquired in a biologically plausible manner? The paper presents a neural network architecture that learns the control operations needed to solve complex working memory tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents WorkMATe, a neural network architecture that integrates gated memory, generic matching, and reinforcement learning to achieve flexible, trainable, and generalizable working memory control.
papers.conclusion: WorkMATe provides a new solution for the neural implementation of flexible memory control and is an important step toward understanding how working memory works.
papers.key_findings:
WorkMATe successfully learns policies for classical working memory tasks (delayed recognition, pro-/anti-saccade) and more complex tasks (12-AX, ABAB ordered recognition).
The model generalizes learned control strategies to new task contexts with novel stimuli.
The gated memory allows independent storage and updating of multiple items in working memory.
Training uses a biologically plausible reinforcement learning rule based on attentional feedback and reward prediction errors.
Compared to a tabular model (simplified PBWM), WorkMATe initially learns slower due to overlapping representations but then performs similarly once stimuli are dissociated.
papers.limitation:
The model is a simplification and does not capture all biological details of the prefrontal cortex and basal ganglia.
The model does not include mechanisms for unsupervised learning or consolidation.
Not every task benefits from gated memory; for example, the pro-/anti-saccade task trained slower with gating.
future_direction: Future work could explore the integration of unsupervised learning mechanisms.
Extending the model to more complex tasks and real-world scenarios.
papers.abstract: Working memory is essential: it serves to guide intelligent behavior of humans and nonhuman primates when task-relevant stimuli are no longer present to the senses. Moreover, complex tasks often require that multiple working memory representations can be flexibly and independently maintained, prioritized, and updated according to changing task demands. Thus far, neural network models of working memory have been unable to offer an integrative account of how such control mechanisms can be acquired in a biologically plausible manner. Here, we present WorkMATe, a neural network architecture that models cognitive control over working memory content and learns the appropriate control operations needed to solve complex working memory tasks. Key components of the model include a gated memory circuit that is controlled by internal actions, encoding sensory information through untrained connections, and a neural circuit that matches sensory inputs to memory content. The network is trained by means of a biologically plausible reinforcement learning rule that relies on attentional feedback and reward prediction errors to guide synaptic updates. We demonstrate that the model successfully acquires policies to solve classical working memory tasks, such as delayed recognition and delayed pro-saccade/anti-saccade tasks. In addition, the model solves much more complex tasks, including the hierarchical 12-AX task or the ABAB ordered recognition task, both of which demand an agent to independently store and updated multiple items separately in memory. Furthermore, the control strategies that the model acquires for these tasks subsequently generalize to new task contexts with novel stimuli, thus bringing symbolic production rule qualities to a neural network architecture. As such, WorkMATe provides a new solution for the neural implementation of flexible memory control.

papers.title: Disentangling Recall and Reasoning in Transformer Models through Layer-wise Attention and Activation Analysis
papers.research_question: Does recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on overlapping or separable internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on partially distinct internal circuits, with early layers supporting recall and deeper layers enabling reasoning, supported by causal evidence from interventions.
papers.conclusion: The Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model develops a hierarchically organized division between recall and reasoning, with early layers for recall and deeper layers for reasoning, supported by task-specific attention heads and MLP neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Layer specialization: early layers (0–6) predominantly support factual recall, while later layers (17–27) concentrate on reasoning.
Head-level differentiation: 74% of attention heads show significant task preferences, with recall-preferring heads in shallower layers and reasoning-preferring heads in deeper layers.
MLP neuron selectivity: roughly one-third of MLP neurons exhibit task-specific activation patterns, with clusters in layers 4 (recall) and 22 (reasoning).
Selective impairment: disabling recall-associated circuits reduces factual accuracy by up to 15% while leaving reasoning unaffected, and vice versa for reasoning circuits.
Consistency: these specialization patterns are statistically stable across cross-validation and robust to normalization choices.
future_direction: Extend experiments to larger, contemporary models such as LLaMA and Mistral.
Expand the dataset to encompass more diverse reasoning phenomena.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models excel at both recall (retrieving memorized facts) and reasoning (performing multi-step inference), but whether these abilities rely on distinct internal mechanisms remains unclear. Distinguishing recall from reasoning is crucial for predicting model generalization, designing targeted evaluations, and building safer interventions that affect one ability without disrupting the other.We approach this question through mechanistic interpretability, using controlled datasets of synthetic linguistic puzzles to probe transformer models at the layer, head, and neuron level. Our pipeline combines activation patching and structured ablations to causally measure component contributions to each task type. Across two model families (Qwen and LLaMA), we find that interventions on distinct layers and attention heads lead to selective impairments: disabling identified "recall circuits" reduces fact-retrieval accuracy by up to 15\% while leaving reasoning intact, whereas disabling "reasoning circuits" reduces multi-step inference by a comparable margin. At the neuron level, we observe task-specific firing patterns, though these effects are less robust, consistent with neuronal polysemanticity.Our results provide the first causal evidence that recall and reasoning rely on separable but interacting circuits in transformer models. These findings advance mechanistic interpretability by linking circuit-level structure to functional specialization and demonstrate how controlled datasets and causal interventions can yield mechanistic insights into model cognition, informing safer deployment of large language models.

papers.title: Attention Heads of Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.core_contribution: This survey paper provides a comprehensive review of research on attention heads in large language models, introducing a novel four-stage framework (Knowledge Recalling, In-Context Identification, Latent Reasoning, Expression Preparation) to categorize attention head functions and summarizing experimental methods for discovering such heads.
papers.conclusion: The survey consolidates research on attention heads in LLMs, providing a framework for understanding their functions and the methods used to discover them, while highlighting the need for further work on complex tasks, unified frameworks, alignment with human cognition, generalizability, multi-collaboration, and theoretical support.
papers.key_findings:
The paper proposes a four-stage framework (Knowledge Recalling, In-Context Identification, Latent Reasoning, Expression Preparation) inspired by human thought to categorize the functions of attention heads in LLMs.
It provides a detailed taxonomy of special attention heads, categorizing them by their roles in the four stages and the LLM architectures where they were discovered.
The survey summarizes experimental methodologies for discovering attention heads into two main categories: Modeling-Free (Modification-Based and Replacement-Based) and Modeling-Required (Training-Required and Training-Free).
It describes how attention heads collaborate across different stages to solve complex tasks, using the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task as an example.
The paper outlines current limitations in the field, such as a focus on simple tasks and lack of unified frameworks, and proposes future research directions.
papers.limitation:
Current research primarily focuses on simple tasks, leaving complex reasoning tasks underexplored.
There is a lack of unified frameworks to comprehensively describe the mechanisms of attention heads.
Aligning LLM mechanisms with human cognitive processes remains a significant challenge.
future_direction: Extending research to more complex tasks and real-world applications.
Developing unified frameworks to comprehensively describe attention head mechanisms.
Enhancing alignment between LLM mechanisms and human cognitive processes.
papers.abstract: Since the advent of ChatGPT, Large Language Models (LLMs) have excelled in various tasks but remain as black-box systems. Understanding the reasoning bottlenecks of LLMs has become a critical challenge, as these limitations are deeply tied to their internal architecture. Among these, attention heads have emerged as a focal point for investigating the underlying mechanics of LLMs. In this survey, we aim to demystify the internal reasoning processes of LLMs by systematically exploring the roles and mechanisms of attention heads. We first introduce a novel four-stage framework inspired by the human thought process: Knowledge Recalling, In-Context Identification, Latent Reasoning, and Expression Preparation. Using this framework, we comprehensively review existing research to identify and categorize the functions of specific attention heads. Additionally, we analyze the experimental methodologies used to discover these special heads, dividing them into two categories: Modeling-Free and Modeling-Required methods. We further summarize relevant evaluation methods and benchmarks. Finally, we discuss the limitations of current research and propose several potential future directions.

papers.title: Cognitive Mirrors: Exploring the Diverse Functional Roles of Attention Heads in LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in large language models specialize for different cognitive functions during complex reasoning tasks, and what are their properties and roles?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel interpretability framework and the CogQA dataset to analyze attention heads in LLMs, revealing that cognitive heads are sparse, functionally specialized, and hierarchically organized, and are crucial for reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a deeper understanding of LLM reasoning and suggests implications for model design, training, and fine-tuning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads exhibit functional specialization for specific cognitive functions (cognitive heads) and are sparse (only a small subset of heads are important for each function).
Cognitive heads are universal across different LLM architectures and model sizes.
Cognitive heads show layered functional organization, with different functions localizing to different layers (e.g., retrieval in middle layers, math in higher layers).
Cognitive heads exhibit functional clustering and hierarchical structure, where lower-level functions (e.g., retrieval) support higher-level reasoning.
Removing cognitive heads degrades performance on corresponding functions, while enhancing them improves reasoning accuracy, demonstrating their causal importance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance in a variety of tasks, but remain largely opaque in terms of their internal mechanisms. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial to improve their reasoning abilities. Drawing inspiration from the interplay between neural processes and human cognition, we propose a novel interpretability framework to systematically analyze the roles and behaviors of attention heads, which are key components of LLMs. We introduce CogQA, a dataset that decomposes complex questions into step-by-step subquestions with a chain-of-thought design, each associated with specific cognitive functions such as retrieval or logical reasoning. By applying a multi-class probing method, we identify the attention heads responsible for these functions. Our analysis across multiple LLM families reveals that attention heads exhibit functional specialization, characterized as cognitive heads. These cognitive heads exhibit several key properties: they are universally sparse, vary in number and distribution across different cognitive functions, and display interactive and hierarchical structures. We further show that cognitive heads play a vital role in reasoning tasks - removing them leads to performance degradation, while augmenting them enhances reasoning accuracy. These insights offer a deeper understanding of LLM reasoning and suggest important implications for model design, training, and fine-tuning strategies.

papers.title: TransformerFAM: Feedback attention is working memory
papers.research_question: How can Transformers be enabled to process indefinitely long sequences? The paper investigates leveraging a feedback loop to create working memory within the Transformer architecture.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TransformerFAM, a novel Transformer architecture that uses a feedback loop to create working memory, enabling processing of indefinitely long sequences with linear complexity and constant memory, without adding new weights.
papers.conclusion: TransformerFAM is a promising architecture that integrates working memory via a feedback loop, enabling Large Language Models to process sequences of unlimited length while maintaining efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
TransformerFAM perfectly solves the PassKey retrieval task with filler contexts up to 260k tokens.
TransformerFAM outperforms TransformerBSWA on a suite of long-context tasks (Isabelle, NarrativeQA, PG-19, ScrollsQasper, ScrollsQuality, XLSum) across 1B, 8B, and 24B model sizes.
TransformerFAM shows scalability, with performance improvements consistent as model size increases from 1B to 24B.
TransformerFAM also improves performance on short-context GPT-3 tasks, suggesting it leads to more efficient contextual representation.
The feedback loop mechanism (FAM) effectively compresses and propagates global contextual information across blocks, acting as a working memory.
papers.limitation: While TransformerFAM shows improvements on long-context tasks, these gains are not yet substantial, highlighting the need for further development and refinement of working memory mechanisms.
future_direction: Further development and refinement of working memory mechanisms in deep learning architectures.
Exploration of attention-based working memory inspired by neuroscience.
papers.abstract: While Transformers have revolutionized deep learning, their quadratic attention complexity hinders their ability to process infinitely long inputs. We propose Feedback Attention Memory (FAM), a novel Transformer architecture that leverages a feedback loop to enable the network to attend to its own latent representations. This design fosters the emergence of working memory within the Transformer, allowing it to process indefinitely long sequences. TransformerFAM requires no additional weights, enabling seamless integration with pre-trained models. Our experiments show that TransformerFAM significantly improves Transformer performance on long-context tasks across various model sizes (1B, 8B, and 24B). These results showcase the potential to empower Large Language Models (LLMs) to process sequences of unlimited length.

papers.title: Emergence of Primacy and Recency Effect in Mamba: A Mechanistic Point of View
papers.research_question: How do primacy and recency effects emerge in the Mamba architecture, and what are the underlying mechanisms for long-term and short-term memory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies three mechanisms underlying primacy and recency effects in Mamba: sparse channels for long-term memory, exponential decay for short-term memory, and delta modulation by input regularity.
papers.conclusion: Mamba exhibits primacy and recency effects due to sparse long-term memory channels, short-term decay dynamics, and input-sensitive gating, challenging the necessity of attention for structured memory.
papers.key_findings:
Primacy effect is supported by a sparse subset of channels in the selective SSM block that persistently encode early tokens.
Recency effect arises from exponential decay in the recurrence, giving more weight to recent inputs.
Adding distractor tokens reduces recency accuracy, showing short-term memory limits.
Memory allocation is modulated by semantic regularity: repeated relations increase forgetting of intermediate items.
The discretization parameter Δt adapts to input frequency, with higher Δt for lower-frequency inputs leading to faster forgetting.
papers.limitation: The study uses a controlled synthetic recall task, which may not generalize to complex natural language tasks.
future_direction: Extending the framework to broader settings and downstream applications
Decoupling the gating factor Δt from input injection to improve memory dynamics
papers.abstract: We study memory in state-space language models using primacy and recency effects as behavioral tools to uncover how information is retained and forgotten over time. Applying structured recall tasks to the Mamba architecture, we observe a consistent U-shaped accuracy profile, indicating strong performance at the beginning and end of input sequences. We identify three mechanisms that give rise to this pattern. First, long-term memory is supported by a sparse subset of channels within the model's selective state space block, which persistently encode early input tokens and are causally linked to primacy effects. Second, short-term memory is governed by delta-modulated recurrence: recent inputs receive more weight due to exponential decay, but this recency advantage collapses when distractor items are introduced, revealing a clear limit to memory depth. Third, we find that memory allocation is dynamically modulated by semantic regularity: repeated relations in the input sequence shift the delta gating behavior, increasing the tendency to forget intermediate items. We validate these findings via targeted ablations and input perturbations on two large-scale Mamba-based language models: one with 1.4B and another with 7B parameters.

papers.title: Learning to Remember, Forget and Ignore using Attention Control in Memory
papers.research_question: How can we design a neural network model that emulates human working memory, specifically focusing on attention control to retain, ignore, or forget information based on relevance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Differentiable Working Memory (DWM) model, which emulates human working memory with a novel attention control mechanism (bookmarks), learns psychology-inspired tasks efficiently, and generalizes to sequences two orders of magnitude longer than training data.
papers.conclusion: The DWM model is a robust and data-efficient working memory model that generalizes well and exhibits interpretable strategies for memory management.
papers.key_findings:
DWM learns working memory tasks faster and generalizes to sequences two orders of magnitude longer than the training sequences.
DWM develops efficient memory usage strategies (e.g., 'Overwrite' and 'Skip') depending on the task and memory constraints.
The attention control mechanism with bookmarks allows the model to retain, ignore, or forget information based on its relevance.
DWM outperforms LSTM and DNC baselines on the proposed working memory tasks in terms of data efficiency and generalization.
The model's behavior is interpretable, showing how it learns to control attention and manage memory resources.
future_direction: Combine the working memory model with long-term memory to solve tasks requiring both working and episodic memory.
papers.abstract: Typical neural networks with external memory do not effectively separate capacity for episodic and working memory as is required for reasoning in humans. Applying knowledge gained from psychological studies, we designed a new model called Differentiable Working Memory (DWM) in order to specifically emulate human working memory. As it shows the same functional characteristics as working memory, it robustly learns psychology inspired tasks and converges faster than comparable state-of-the-art models. Moreover, the DWM model successfully generalizes to sequences two orders of magnitude longer than the ones used in training. Our in-depth analysis shows that the behavior of DWM is interpretable and that it learns to have fine control over memory, allowing it to retain, ignore or forget information based on its relevance.

papers.title: Neural Mechanisms of Working Memory Accuracy Revealed by Recurrent Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) trained on spatial working memory tasks reveal the neural mechanisms of working memory accuracy, particularly the relationship between delay period activity and behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that RNNs trained on working memory tasks spontaneously develop delay period activity resembling prefrontal cortex persistent activity, and that drift in this activity is causal to behavioral accuracy, supporting the computational efficiency of delay period activity for working memory.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that RNNs can reveal computational principles of working memory and that delay period activity is computationally efficient for maintaining working memory, as evidenced by unbiased optimization in artificial networks.
papers.key_findings:
RNNs trained on working memory tasks develop persistent delay period activity similar to prefrontal neurons.
The weight matrix that emerges after training shows a structure where units with similar tuning are more strongly connected, resembling bump attractor models.
Delay period activity in RNN units is predictive of behavior: correct trials have higher delay activity for preferred locations.
The variability of RNN units (Fano factor) shows an M-shaped curve as a function of tuning, similar to prefrontal cortex.
The correlation between firing rate and saccade deviation indicates that drift in delay activity determines behavioral accuracy.
papers.limitation:
RNNs are not a precise replica of the brain; they are smaller, have less variability, and exhibit more prominent oscillatory dynamics than the prefrontal cortex.
The study did not examine opposing models of working memory, such as those relying on synaptic mechanisms.
future_direction: Understanding more complex working memory tasks, such as object working memory.
Studying tasks that require manipulation of information in working memory.
Investigating tasks probing the capacity limitation of human working memory.
papers.abstract: Understanding the neural mechanisms of working memory has been a long-standing Neuroscience goal. Bump attractor models have been used to simulate persistent activity generated in the prefrontal cortex during working memory tasks and to study the relationship between activity and behavior. How realistic the assumptions of these models are has been a matter of debate. Here, we relied on an alternative strategy to gain insights into the computational principles behind the generation of persistent activity and on whether current models capture some universal computational principles. We trained Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to perform spatial working memory tasks and examined what aspects of RNN activity accounted for working memory performance. Furthermore, we compared activity in fully trained networks and immature networks, achieving only imperfect performance. We thus examined the relationship between the trial-to-trial variability of responses simulated by the network and different aspects of unit activity as a way of identifying the critical parameters of memory maintenance. Properties that spontaneously emerged in the artificial network strongly resembled persistent activity of prefrontal neurons. Most importantly, these included drift of network activity during the course of a trial that was causal to the behavior of the network. As a consequence, delay period firing rate and behavior were positively correlated, in strong analogy to experimental results from the prefrontal cortex. These findings reveal that delay period activity is computationally efficient in maintaining working memory, as evidenced by unbiased optimization of parameters in artificial neural networks, oblivious to the properties of prefrontal neurons.

papers.title: The Reasoning-Memorization Interplay in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation, and can we identify linear features that mediate this interplay?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies linear reasoning features (LiReFs) in the residual stream of LLMs that mediate the switch between reasoning and memorization, and shows that intervening on these features can improve reasoning performance and generalizability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that linear reasoning features in the residual stream mediate the reasoning-memorization interplay in LLMs, and that targeted intervention on these features can enhance reasoning performance and generalizability, offering insights for more robust and interpretable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Linear Reasoning Features (LiReFs) can be extracted from the residual stream by contrasting reasoning-intensive and memory-intensive questions.
LiReFs separate questions by their required capability (reasoning vs. memory) across domains and languages.
The activation along LiReFs correlates with the reasoning score assigned by GPT-4o, indicating a spectrum from memory to reasoning.
Inference-time intervention on LiReFs (adding or ablating) can improve model performance on both memory and reasoning tasks.
LiReF intervention enhances genuine reasoning generalizability, as shown on GSM-Symbolic, and reduces reasoning errors.
papers.limitation: The study's definition of memorization as poor generalizability may not capture other forms of memorization (e.g., counterfactual memorization).
future_direction: Investigate whether perturbational and counterfactual memorization are mechanistically equivalent and mediated by LiReFs.
Extend the LiReF analysis to more models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on a variety of reasoning benchmarks, but previous studies suggest they sometimes struggle to generalize to unseen questions, potentially due to over-reliance on memorized training examples. However, the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation remain unclear. In this work, we provide a mechanistic understanding of LLMs' reasoning-memorization dynamics by identifying a set of linear features in the model's residual stream that govern the balance between genuine reasoning and memory recall. These features not only distinguish reasoning tasks from memory-intensive ones but can also be manipulated to causally influence model performance on reasoning tasks. Additionally, we show that intervening in these reasoning features helps the model more accurately activate the most relevant problem-solving capabilities during answer generation. Our findings offer new insights into the underlying mechanisms of reasoning and memory in LLMs and pave the way for the development of more robust and interpretable generative AI systems.

papers.title: Understanding Factual Recall in Transformers via Associative Memories
papers.research_question: How do transformers store factual information and what is their storage capacity?
papers.core_contribution: Shallow transformers can achieve near-optimal storage capacity for factual recall by using associative memories in both self-attention and MLP components, with a trade-off between them.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can efficiently store factual information using associative memories implemented in self-attention and MLP components.
papers.key_findings:
Linear and MLP associative memories can store a number of associations proportional to their parameter count.
A one-layer transformer can achieve 100% accuracy on a synthetic factual recall task when either the total self-attention parameters or MLP parameters scale linearly with the number of facts.
The transformer exhibits sequential learning dynamics during training, with an initial 'hallucination' stage.
The storage constructions are optimal up to logarithmic factors.
papers.limitation: The linear associative memory construction requires the association function to be injective for optimal capacity.
papers.abstract: Large language models have demonstrated an impressive ability to perform factual recall. Prior work has found that transformers trained on factual recall tasks can store information at a rate proportional to their parameter count. In our work, we show that shallow transformers can use a combination of associative memories to obtain such near optimal storage capacity. We begin by proving that the storage capacities of both linear and MLP associative memories scale linearly with parameter count. We next introduce a synthetic factual recall task, and prove that a transformer with a single layer of self-attention followed by an MLP can obtain 100% accuracy on the task whenever either the total number of self-attention parameters or MLP parameters scales (up to log factors) linearly with the number of facts. In particular, the transformer can trade off between using the value matrices or the MLP as an associative memory to store the dataset of facts. We complement these expressivity results with an analysis of the gradient flow trajectory of a simplified linear attention model trained on our factual recall task, where we show that the model exhibits sequential learning behavior.

papers.title: Geometry of naturalistic object representations in recurrent neural network models of working memory
papers.research_question: How do task-optimized RNNs select and dynamically maintain task-relevant properties of naturalistic objects during working memory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that RNNs trained on multi-task N-back tasks use chronological memory subspaces to maintain naturalistic object information, and that gated RNNs use task-specific subspaces while vanilla RNNs use shared subspaces.
papers.conclusion: Goal-driven RNNs employ chronological memory subspaces to track naturalistic object information over short time spans, providing testable predictions for neural data.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-task RNNs represent both task-relevant and irrelevant object information simultaneously.
Vanilla RNNs encode object properties within a subspace shared across tasks, while GRUs and LSTMs use highly task-specific subspaces.
Object features are less orthogonalized in the RNNs' hidden dynamics compared to perceptual representations from the CNN.
RNNs solve the N-back task by using chronological memory subspaces to separate object representations presented across time, supporting resource-based over slot-based models of working memory.
The transformation of object information from encoding to memory subspaces is shared across different stimuli but distinct across time steps.
papers.limitation:
Results are specific to the N-back task structure; it's uncertain if similar strategies emerge in other working memory tasks.
Did not analyze the representational geometry for novel objects or investigate reasons for diminished performance with them.
Findings are restricted to commonly used RNN architectures (vanilla RNN, GRU, LSTM).
Did not explore how scaling the network size might influence the results.
future_direction: Exploring whether other neural network architectures yield similar or distinct representational patterns.
Investigating how scaling the network size might influence the strategies employed by models.
Testing the predictions about chronological memory subspaces with neural data in humans.
papers.abstract: Working memory is a central cognitive ability crucial for intelligent decision-making. Recent experimental and computational work studying working memory has primarily used categorical (i.e., one-hot) inputs, rather than ecologically relevant, multidimensional naturalistic ones. Moreover, studies have primarily investigated working memory during single or few cognitive tasks. As a result, an understanding of how naturalistic object information is maintained in working memory in neural networks is still lacking. To bridge this gap, we developed sensory-cognitive models, comprising a convolutional neural network (CNN) coupled with a recurrent neural network (RNN), and trained them on nine distinct N-back tasks using naturalistic stimuli. By examining the RNN's latent space, we found that: (1) Multi-task RNNs represent both task-relevant and irrelevant information simultaneously while performing tasks; (2) The latent subspaces used to maintain specific object properties in vanilla RNNs are largely shared across tasks, but highly task-specific in gated RNNs such as GRU and LSTM; (3) Surprisingly, RNNs embed objects in new representational spaces in which individual object features are less orthogonalized relative to the perceptual space; (4) The transformation of working memory encodings (i.e., embedding of visual inputs in the RNN latent space) into memory was shared across stimuli, yet the transformations governing the retention of a memory in the face of incoming distractor stimuli were distinct across time. Our findings indicate that goal-driven RNNs employ chronological memory subspaces to track information over short time spans, enabling testable predictions with neural data.

papers.title: Characterizing Mechanisms for Factual Recall in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do distributional and mechanistic factors determine a language model's behavior when there is a conflict between memorized facts and in-context information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies specific attention heads that control the use of memorized vs. in-context information and shows that scaling these heads at runtime can dynamically control model behavior without parameter updates.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that frequency and specific attention heads influence factual recall and provides a proof of concept for controlling model behavior dynamically at runtime.
papers.key_findings:
The frequency of the country and in-context city in pretraining data affects the model's tendency to use memorized vs. in-context information.
Larger models are more likely to use memorized answers, especially for frequent terms.
Individual attention heads can be identified that promote either memorized or in-context answers.
Scaling down a memory head can increase the rate of in-context answers to 88% on the world capitals task.
The memory head promotes geography-related tokens, indicating domain specificity, and does not generalize well to other factual domains.
papers.limitation: The dataset used is templated and limited to the domain of country-capital relationships, so findings may not generalize to arbitrary contexts.
future_direction: Developing more general techniques for controlling the use of context vs. memorized information in arbitrary tasks.
Discovering more general mechanisms beyond domain-specific heads.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) often must integrate facts they memorized in pretraining with new information that appears in a given context. These two sources can disagree, causing competition within the model, and it is unclear how an LM will resolve the conflict. On a dataset that queries for knowledge of world capitals, we investigate both distributional and mechanistic determinants of LM behavior in such situations. Specifically, we measure the proportion of the time an LM will use a counterfactual prefix (e.g., “The capital of Poland is London”) to overwrite what it learned in pretraining (“Warsaw”). On Pythia and GPT2, the training frequency of both the query country (”Poland”) and the in-context city (”London”) highly affect the models’ likelihood of using the counterfactual. We then use head attribution to identify individual attention heads that either promote the memorized answer or the in-context answer in the logits. By scaling up or down the value vector of these heads, we can control the likelihood of using the in-context answer on new data. This method can increase the rate of generating the in-context answer to 88% of the time simply by scaling a single head at runtime. Our work contributes to a body of evidence showing that we can often localize model behaviors to specific components and provides a proof of concept for how future methods might control model behavior dynamically at runtime.

papers.title: Retentive or Forgetful? Diving into the Knowledge Memorizing Mechanism of Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the memorizing dynamics of language models, and how does pre-training affect their memory ability?
papers.core_contribution: Pre-training transforms language models from forgetful to retentive by enabling long-term memory formation, influenced by knowledge relevance and diversity.
papers.conclusion: Vanilla language models are forgetful, pre-training leads to retentive models, and knowledge relevance and diversification significantly influence memory formation.
papers.key_findings:
Vanilla language models are forgetful with short memory duration and limited capacity.
Pre-trained language models are retentive and can gradually memorize knowledge through repetitive learning.
Pre-training is crucial for developing long-term memory ability in language models.
There is memory competition between highly relevant knowledge types in pre-trained models.
Lack of knowledge diversity causes memory collapse in early learning stages.
future_direction: Investigate the underlying reasons for the forgetful-retentive transition during pre-training.
Explore other critical factors affecting memorization beyond pre-training and diversity.
Compare memorization mechanisms between language models and the human brain.
papers.abstract: Memory is one of the most essential cognitive functions serving as a repository of world knowledge and episodes of activities. In recent years, large-scale pre-trained language models have shown remarkable memorizing ability. On the contrary, vanilla neural networks without pre-training have been long observed suffering from the catastrophic forgetting problem. To investigate such a retentive-forgetful contradiction and understand the memory mechanism of language models, we conduct thorough experiments by controlling the target knowledge types, the learning strategies and the learning schedules. We find that: 1) Vanilla language models are forgetful; 2) Pre-training leads to retentive language models; 3) Knowledge relevance and diversification significantly influence the memory formation. These conclusions are useful for understanding the abilities of pre-trained language models and shed light on designing and evaluating new learning and inference algorithms of language models.

papers.title: Memorization Without Overfitting: Analyzing the Training Dynamics of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do memorization and forgetting dynamics in language models change during training, and how do they depend on factors like model size, dataset size, and learning rate?
papers.core_contribution: Larger language models memorize training data faster and forget less throughout training, with nouns and numbers being memorized more quickly than other parts of speech.
papers.conclusion: Memorization dynamics are a critical metric for understanding language model training, with larger models exhibiting faster memorization and less forgetting, highlighting the importance of analyzing memorization alongside cross-entropy loss.
papers.key_findings:
Larger language models memorize training data faster across various settings (causal and masked LM, different dataset sizes).
Larger models can memorize a larger portion of the data before overfitting occurs.
Forgetting curves approach a baseline (the forgetting baseline), and this baseline increases with model scale, meaning larger models forget less.
Nouns and numbers are memorized much faster than other parts of speech, acting as unique identifiers for training examples.
Adding unique identifiers (like document IDs) to training examples increases memorization speed.
papers.limitation:
The exact memorization metric (Definition 1) ignores model confidence and does not normalize for duplication in the training set.
The focus on exact memorization may not capture all aspects of privacy, as it only considers verbatim output of sensitive information.
future_direction: Understanding the structure of the forgetting baseline, e.g., what types of tokens (parts of speech, synonyms, facts) are memorized in the baseline.
Analyzing memorization dynamics as a critical metric when scaling up language models, beyond just cross-entropy loss.
papers.abstract: Despite their wide adoption, the underlying training and memorization dynamics of very large language models is not well understood. We empirically study exact memorization in causal and masked language modeling, across model sizes and throughout the training process.
