We measure the effects of dataset size, learning rate, and model size on memorization, finding that larger language models memorize training data faster across all settings. Surprisingly, we show that larger models can memorize a larger portion of the data before over-fitting and tend to forget less throughout the training process. We also analyze the memorization dynamics of different parts of speech and find that models memorize nouns and numbers first; we hypothesize and provide empirical evidence that nouns and numbers act as a unique identifier for memorizing individual training examples. Together, these findings present another piece of the broader puzzle of trying to understand what actually improves as models get bigger.

papers.title: Retrieval Head Mechanistically Explains Long-Context Factuality
papers.research_question: How do long-context language models retrieve relevant information from arbitrary locations within the input?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers and characterizes 'retrieval heads', a sparse set of attention heads responsible for retrieving information from long contexts, and shows they are universal, intrinsic, and causally important for factuality and reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Retrieval heads implement a conditional copy algorithm and are the primary reason why long-context models can pass the Needle-in-a-Haystack test; their activation explains model factuality versus hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
Retrieval heads are universal and sparse, existing in all tested long-context models and constituting less than 5% of attention heads.
Retrieval heads are intrinsic, already present in base models and reused in derived models (e.g., via continued pretraining or fine-tuning).
Retrieval heads are dynamically activated based on the specific tokens and context required for retrieval.
Retrieval heads are causal; pruning them leads to retrieval failure and hallucination, while pruning non-retrieval heads does not.
Retrieval heads strongly influence chain-of-thought reasoning tasks, which require frequent reference to input information, but have less impact on tasks relying on internal knowledge.
future_direction: Fostering future research on reducing hallucination, improving reasoning, and compressing the KV cache.
Discovering more algorithm and functionalities implemented by other types of attention heads.
Applying insights to KV cache compression by pruning non-retrieval head caches.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent progress in long-context language models, it remains elusive how transformer-based models exhibit the capability to retrieve relevant information from arbitrary locations within the long context. This paper aims to address this question. Our systematic investigation across a wide spectrum of models reveals that a special type of attention heads are largely responsible for retrieving information, which we dub retrieval heads. We identify intriguing properties of retrieval heads:(1) universal: all the explored models with long-context capability have a set of retrieval heads; (2) sparse: only a small portion (less than 5\%) of the attention heads are retrieval. (3) intrinsic: retrieval heads already exist in models pretrained with short context. When extending the context length by continual pretraining, it is still the same set of heads that perform information retrieval. (4) dynamically activated: take Llama-2 7B for example, 12 retrieval heads always attend to the required information no matter how the context is changed. The rest of the retrieval heads are activated in different contexts. (5) causal: completely pruning retrieval heads leads to failure in retrieving relevant information and results in hallucination, while pruning random non-retrieval heads does not affect the model's retrieval ability. We further show that retrieval heads strongly influence chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, where the model needs to frequently refer back the question and previously-generated context. Conversely, tasks where the model directly generates the answer using its intrinsic knowledge are less impacted by masking out retrieval heads. These observations collectively explain which internal part of the model seeks information from the input tokens. We believe our insights will foster future research on reducing hallucination, improving reasoning, and compressing the KV cache.

papers.title: Episodic grammar: a computational model of the interaction between episodic and semantic memory in language processing
papers.research_question: How do episodic and semantic memory interact in language processing, and can this be modeled computationally for syntactic parsing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an episodic grammar model that integrates semantic and episodic memory for syntactic parsing, achieving competitive performance on the WSJ corpus.
papers.conclusion: The episodic grammar framework unifies rule-based and exemplar-based approaches to syntax within a neural perspective, interpreting them as semantic and episodic memory respectively.
papers.key_findings:
The episodic grammar model improves parsing performance over baseline PCFG models.
Left-corner derivation strategy outperforms top-down derivation in the episodic framework.
Including discontiguous episodes provides minor improvements in F-score.
The model's performance is robust across different n-best list sizes for reranking.
Episodic grammar offers a content-addressable memory approach that avoids large grammar sizes.
papers.limitation: Reranking has limitations as an assessment of the model's performance due to upper and lower bound precision and recall scores from the third-party parser.
future_direction: Developing a full episodic chart parser that computes parse probabilities online via spreading activation.
Integrating the model with the HPN network in a connectionist framework for unsupervised learning.
Investigating syntactic priming effects and recency effects in sentence processing.
papers.abstract: We present a model of the interaction of semantic and episodic memory in language processing. Our work shows how language processing can be understood in terms of memory retrieval. We point out that the perceived dichotomy between rule-based versus exemplar-based language modelling can be interpreted in a neuro-biological perspective in terms of the interaction between a semantic memory system that encodes linguistic knowledge in the form of abstract rules, and an episodic memory that stores concrete linguistic events. We implement the idea of a semantic-episodic memory integration in a probabilistic grammar, and evaluate its performance as a syntactic parser on corpora of natural language. Our labeled precision and recall results are competitive with state-of-the-art syntactic parsers, with F-scores up to 90.68 on section 22 of the Penn WSJ corpus.

papers.title: How Do Multilingual Language Models Remember Facts?
papers.research_question: How do factual recall mechanisms in English LLMs generalize to multilingual LLMs, and when does language play a role in recall?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that factual recall mechanisms in English LLMs generalize to multilingual LLMs with variations, and reveals that the last token acts as a function vector encoding relation and language, composed in two stages in decoder-only models.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for factual recall, indicating that knowledge evaluation and editing methods need to be adapted for multilingual settings.
papers.key_findings:
The early MLP site for subject enrichment is present in multilingual LLMs, but the late site involves both MLP and attention, unlike English LLMs where only attention dominates.
Subject information flows similarly to monolingual models, but non-subject token flow differs.
In multilingual decoder-only LLMs, both feed-forward and attention sublayers contribute to object extraction, unlike in English autoregressive LLMs where attention modules dominate.
The last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV) encoding both the relation and the output language.
In decoder-only LLMs, the FV is constructed in two distinct phases: first encoding the relation, then incorporating the language.
future_direction: Developing knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition methods tailored for multilingual LLMs
Studying how the function vector is altered across languages to understand if models think in English
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) store and retrieve vast amounts of factual knowledge acquired during pre-training. Prior research has localized and identified mechanisms behind knowledge recall; however, it has only focused on English monolingual models. The question of how these mechanisms generalize to non-English languages and multilingual LLMs remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap by conducting a comprehensive analysis of three multilingual LLMs. First, we show that previously identified recall mechanisms in English largely apply to multilingual contexts, with nuances based on language and architecture. Next, through patching intermediate representations, we localize the role of language during recall, finding that subject enrichment is language-independent, while object extraction is language-dependent. Additionally, we discover that the last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV), encoding both the language of the query and the content to be extracted from the subject. Furthermore, in decoder-only LLMs, FVs compose these two pieces of information in two separate stages. These insights reveal unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for recalling information, highlighting the need for new methodologies -- such as knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition -- that are specifically tailored for multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: Are Sixteen Heads Really Better than One?
papers.research_question: What is the contribution of individual attention heads in multi-head attention models, and can a large percentage be pruned at test time without significantly impacting performance?
papers.core_contribution: Many attention heads in trained multi-head attention models are redundant and can be pruned without significant performance loss, with encoder-decoder attention being more reliant on multiple heads than self-attention.
papers.conclusion: Multi-head attention does not always fully leverage its theoretical expressiveness, and pruning heads can improve inference efficiency without harming performance, offering insights for more parameter-efficient models.
papers.key_findings:
Most attention heads can be individually removed at test time without a statistically significant drop in performance.
Some entire attention layers can be reduced to a single head without impacting performance.
A greedy pruning algorithm based on a gradient-derived importance score can remove 20-40% of heads without noticeable performance degradation.
Encoder-decoder attention layers are much more sensitive to pruning than self-attention layers.
The distinction between important and unimportant heads increases as training progresses, suggesting training dynamics play a role.
future_direction: A more principled investigation of the training dynamics of head importance.
Inspiring models that invest their parameters and attention more efficiently.
papers.abstract: Attention is a powerful and ubiquitous mechanism for allowing neural models to focus on particular salient pieces of information by taking their weighted average when making predictions. In particular, multi-headed attention is a driving force behind many recent state-of-the-art NLP models such as Transformer-based MT models and BERT. These models apply multiple attention mechanisms in parallel, with each attention "head" potentially focusing on different parts of the input, which makes it possible to express sophisticated functions beyond the simple weighted average. In this paper we make the surprising observation that even if models have been trained using multiple heads, in practice, a large percentage of attention heads can be removed at test time without significantly impacting performance. In fact, some layers can even be reduced to a single head. We further examine greedy algorithms for pruning down models, and the potential speed, memory efficiency, and accuracy improvements obtainable therefrom. Finally, we analyze the results with respect to which parts of the model are more reliant on having multiple heads, and provide precursory evidence that training dynamics play a role in the gains provided by multi-head attention.

papers.title: Sequence-to-Sequence Models with Attention Mechanistically Map to the Architecture of Human Memory Search
papers.research_question: Why do human memory systems use context-based architectures, and are these architectures optimal? The paper investigates the convergence between sequence-to-sequence models with attention (from machine translation) and context-based models of human memory.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sequence-to-sequence models with attention mechanistically map to the Context Maintenance and Retrieval (CMR) model of human memory, and implements such a model as an interpretable cognitive model that captures human free recall behavior and provides insights into memory search dynamics.
papers.conclusion: Seq2seq models with attention provide a powerful framework for modeling human memory search, offering interpretability and flexibility, and the convergence suggests functional rationality in human memory architecture.
papers.key_findings:
Seq2seq models with attention mathematically map to the CMR model and capture human free recall behavior as effectively as CMR.
The optimized seq2seq model exhibits optimal recall behavior similar to rational-CMR.
Intermediate training stages show recency and backward contiguity effects similar to average human behavior.
Working memory capacity (hidden dimension size) affects how primacy is achieved: with small hidden dimensions, attention shifts to the beginning; with large, primacy is maintained in the hidden state.
Ablation of attention mimics memory deficits in medial temporal lobe amnesia patients.
papers.abstract: Past work has long recognized the important role of context in guiding how humans search their memory. While context-based memory models can explain many memory phenomena, it remains unclear why humans develop such architectures over possible alternatives in the first place. In this work, we demonstrate that foundational architectures in neural machine translation -- specifically, recurrent neural network (RNN)-based sequence-to-sequence models with attention -- exhibit mechanisms that directly correspond to those specified in the Context Maintenance and Retrieval (CMR) model of human memory. Since neural machine translation models have evolved to optimize task performance, their convergence with human memory models provides a deeper understanding of the functional role of context in human memory, as well as presenting new ways to model human memory. Leveraging this convergence, we implement a neural machine translation model as a cognitive model of human memory search that is both interpretable and capable of capturing complex dynamics of learning. We show that our model accounts for both averaged and optimal human behavioral patterns as effectively as context-based memory models. Further, we demonstrate additional strengths of the proposed model by evaluating how memory search performance emerges from the interaction of different model components.

papers.title: Taming Knowledge Conflicts in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models handle knowledge conflicts between parametric memory and contextual information, and can we design a method to steer them towards either source without fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory in attention heads and proposes JUICE, a test-time attention intervention method that steers LMs toward either parametric or contextual knowledge without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: JUICE sets a new state-of-the-art for handling knowledge conflicts, offering robust generalization across domains and conflict types, and is supported by theoretical analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads exhibit inconsistent behaviors under different degrees of knowledge conflict, challenging the notion of exclusive 'memory heads' and 'context heads'.
Combining individually effective interventions can lead to counteracting effects due to superposition.
JUICE achieves state-of-the-art performance in steering LMs towards parametric or contextual knowledge across diverse datasets and models.
JUICE is effective even with a very small head identification set (e.g., 4 samples).
The dual-run design of JUICE mitigates superposition effects and outperforms single-run interventions.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) often encounter knowledge conflicts when parametric memory contradicts contextual knowledge. Previous works attribute this conflict to the interplay between "memory heads" and "context heads", attention heads assumed to promote either memory or context exclusively. In this study, we go beyond this fundamental assumption by uncovering a critical phenomenon we term the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory, where highly influential attention heads simultaneously contribute to both memory and context. Building upon this insight, we propose Just Run Twice (JuICE), a test-time attention intervention method that steers LMs toward either parametric beliefs or contextual knowledge without requiring fine-tuning. JuICE identifies a set of reliable attention heads and leverages a dual-run approach to mitigate the superposition effects. Extensive experiments across 11 datasets and 6 model architectures demonstrate that JuICE sets the new state-of-the-art performance and robust generalization, achieving significant and consistent improvement across different domains under various conflict types. Finally, we theoretically analyze knowledge conflict and the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory in attention heads, which further elucidates the effectiveness of JuICE in these settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/GaotangLi/JUICE.

papers.title: Memorization in Attention-only Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the memorization capacity of attention-only Transformers for any context size, and how can we extend the theory to include approximate memorization of distributions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that a one-layer attention-only Transformer can memorize H*d_h + d associations, improving prior bounds, and introduces the distribution task for approximate memorization.
papers.conclusion: The paper advances the state of the art in exact memorization for attention-only Transformers and introduces memorization in distribution with theoretical bounds.
papers.key_findings:
A one-layer attention-only Transformer can memorize at least H*d_h + d associations.
Empirical scaling laws show linear scaling in the number of heads H and quadratic scaling in head dimension d_h when embedding dimension d is fixed.
The paper introduces the distribution task for memorizing distributions over next tokens and provides upper and lower bounds on the KL-divergence.
Under optimization constraints, attention-only Transformers are better at memorization than MLP-based Transformers.
The paper provides a novel proof that overcomes the limitation of prior work requiring context size to be smaller than embedding dimension.
papers.limitation:
The constant C in the bound depends on the singular value decomposition of W_V A and is hard to control effectively.
The construction for the skip connection requires taking λ→∞, leading to an approximation error γ.
future_direction: Deeper understanding of the expressivity of the attention mechanism.
Characterizing which distributions are in the closure of M(N,S,d).
papers.abstract: Recent research has explored the memorization capacity of multi-head attention, but these findings are constrained by unrealistic limitations on the context size. We present a novel proof for language-based Transformers that extends the current hypothesis to any context size. Our approach improves upon the state-of-the-art by achieving more effective exact memorization with an attention layer, while also introducing the concept of approximate memorization of distributions. Through experimental validation, we demonstrate that our proposed bounds more accurately reflect the true memorization capacity of language models, and provide a precise comparison with prior work.

papers.title: Recurrent neural network models for working memory of continuous variables: activity manifolds, connectivity patterns, and dynamic codes
papers.research_question: How do recurrent neural networks represent and maintain multiple continuous variables in working memory, and what are the geometric and connectivity properties of such representations?
papers.core_contribution: RNNs trained on a working memory task use a Clifford torus geometry to store two orientations in orthogonal subspaces, employ local-excitation/global-inhibition connectivity, and use dynamic coding to prevent overwriting; noise and ordinal output are necessary to reproduce human psychophysics data.
papers.conclusion: RNNs provide insights into neural computations for working memory, bridging behavior to connectivity, and suitable inductive biases (noise, ordinal output) are important for uncovering brain-like computation.
papers.key_findings:
The activity manifold for two remembered orientations resembles a Clifford torus, which stores the orientations in orthogonal subspaces.
The Clifford-torus-like manifold is realized by two different sets of locally-excitatory/globally-inhibitory connectivity patterns.
Dynamic coding, where units change their tuning over time, prevents the new sensory input from overwriting the previously stored memory.
Not all RNNs reproduce human behavior; injecting noise during training and including an ordinal output are required to match human psychophysical data.
The high-to-low-level decoding scheme (using ordinal relationship to constrain absolute orientation recall) emerges in RNNs trained with noise, explaining human data.
papers.abstract: Many daily activities and psychophysical experiments involve keeping multiple items in working memory. When items take continuous values (e.g., orientation, contrast, length, loudness) they must be stored in a continuous structure of appropriate dimensions. We investigate how this structure is represented in neural circuits by training recurrent networks to report two previously shown stimulus orientations. We find the activity manifold for the two orientations resembles a Clifford torus. Although a Clifford and standard torus (the surface of a donut) are topologically equivalent, they have important functional differences. A Clifford torus treats the two orientations equally and keeps them in orthogonal subspaces, as demanded by the task, whereas a standard torus does not. We find and characterize the connectivity patterns that support the Clifford torus. Moreover, in addition to attractors that store information via persistent activity, our networks also use a dynamic code where units change their tuning to prevent new sensory input from overwriting the previously stored one. We argue that such dynamic codes are generally required whenever multiple inputs enter a memory system via shared connections. Finally, we apply our framework to a human psychophysics experiment in which subjects reported two remembered orientations. By varying the training conditions of the RNNs, we test and support the hypothesis that human behavior is a product of both neural noise and reliance on the more stable and behaviorally relevant memory of the ordinal relationship between the two orientations. This suggests that suitable inductive biases in RNNs are important for uncovering how the human brain implements working memory. Together, these results offer an understanding of the neural computations underlying a class of visual decoding tasks, bridging the scales from human behavior to synaptic connectivity.

papers.title: Memory Retrieval in Online Sentence Parsing: Empirical Evidence, Computational Modelling, and Simulations
papers.research_question: How does memory retrieval work during online sentence parsing, and under what conditions does similarity-based interference occur?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Revision Integrated Cue-Based (RICB) model, which successfully predicts similarity-based interference data in floating quantifier processing, emphasizing structural information and revision.
papers.conclusion: The RICB model accounts for the data and underscores the importance of structural information and revision in memory retrieval during real-time sentence processing.
papers.key_findings:
Similarity-based interference was observed in ungrammatical sentences but not in grammatical sentences.
The interference patterns were not consistent with existing theories and models.
The RICB model, which assumes heavy weighting of structural cues and includes revision, predicts the observed data.
The results highlight the central role of structural information and revision in memory retrieval during sentence processing.
papers.limitation:
Detecting similarity-based interference requires large sample sizes, particularly in grammatical sentences.
The patterns of interference were not consistent with existing theories and models.
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper reports two experiments (Experiments 1 and 2) and computational simulations designed to investigate and model memory retrieval processes during real-time sentence processing. Central to this study is the hypothesis that linguistic information serves as a cue to retrieve target representations from memory during dependency formation. The basis for this cue-based memory retrieval stems from research showing that non-target representations that match a set of retrieval cues interfere with target retrieval. The susceptibility to this similarity-based interference has been debated in the sentence processing literature, and various hypotheses and models have been formulated and developed. This issue is addressed empirically in Experiments 1 and 2, which investigated similarity-based interference in sentences with a floating quantifier. Bayesian linear mixed models and Bayes factor analyses suggested similarity-based interference. However, the patterns of interference were not consistent with existing theories and models. To reconcile these findings within the framework of cue-based memory retrieval, this paper implements the Revision Integrated Cue-Based (RICB) model based on the ACT–R architecture. This model assumes that structural information is heavily weighted and incorporates the notions of initial retrieval and revision. The results of the simulations indicate that the RICB model successfully predicts the observed data, highlighting the central role of structural information and revision in memory retrieval during real-time sentence processing.

papers.title: Recurrent neural networks with transient trajectory explain working memory encoding mechanisms
papers.research_question: Whether working memory is better encoded by transient trajectories or by persistent activities in recurrent neural networks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a transient-trajectory-based RNN (TRNN) that better replicates biological working memory activity patterns and demonstrates superior performance in working memory tasks compared to vanilla RNNs, supporting the transient activity theory of working memory.
papers.conclusion: The study provides evidence supporting transient trajectory encoding as a mechanistic explanation for working memory, based on the biological plausibility and superior task performance of TRNNs compared to attractor-based vanilla RNNs.
papers.key_findings:
TRNNs reproduce transient trajectory activity patterns that closely resemble animal recordings, as measured by the transient index (TI).
TRNNs can maintain working memory for variable delay periods by recruiting additional neurons for longer delays.
TRNNs exhibit higher information richness (entropy) and lower energy consumption (average squared firing rate) compared to vanilla RNNs.
TRNNs achieve better performance in reinforcement learning tasks requiring working memory, such as direction-following and water maze navigation.
The transient trajectory encoding in TRNNs is supported by asymmetric recurrent connections that facilitate sequential activity.
papers.limitation:
The use of rate-coded neurons assumes memory is stored in firing rates and does not consider the potential role of spike timing coding.
In the water maze task, the poor performance of vanilla RNNs may be due to factors other than memory (e.g., navigation or movement execution), making direct comparison of memory abilities less valid.
future_direction: Extending the approach to combine working memory research with long-term memory research to study information transfer and interaction.
Using spiking neural networks (SNNs) for simulation to better capture potential spike timing mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Whether working memory (WM) is encoded by persistent activity using attractors or by dynamic activity using transient trajectories has been debated for decades in both experimental and modeling studies, and a consensus has not been reached. Even though many recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have been proposed to simulate WM, most networks are designed to match respective experimental observations and show either transient or persistent activities. Those few which consider networks with both activity patterns have not attempted to directly compare their memory capabilities. In this study, we build transient-trajectory-based RNNs (TRNNs) and compare them to vanilla RNNs with more persistent activities. The TRNN incorporates biologically plausible modifications, including self-inhibition, sparse connection and hierarchical topology. Besides activity patterns resembling animal recordings and retained versatility to variable encoding time, TRNNs show better performance in delayed choice and spatial memory reinforcement learning tasks. Therefore, this study provides evidence supporting the transient activity theory to explain the WM mechanism from the model designing point of view.

papers.title: Time Course MechInterp: Analyzing the Evolution of Components and Knowledge in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do the components (attention heads and FFNs) responsible for factual knowledge in a large language model evolve during pre-training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that during pre-training, LLMs start with general-purpose components that later specialize, with attention heads showing high role turnover while FFNs remain stable.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a mechanistic view of how factual knowledge forms in LLMs, showing a dynamic specialization process for attention heads and stable FFNs.
papers.key_findings:
Location-based relations converge to high accuracy earlier in training than name-based relations.
Attention heads initially depend on general-purpose roles and later specialize as training progresses.
Attention heads exhibit high role turnover, especially answer-specific heads.
FFNs remain more stable throughout training, acting as a steady processing backbone.
Once the model reliably predicts answers, some components are repurposed, suggesting an adaptive learning process.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints prevented analysis at the neuron level, potentially missing finer-grained switching behaviors.
The dataset is limited to English and covers only location-based and name-based relations, limiting generalizability.
The interpretability framework (Information Flow Routes) may miss finer-grained interactions compared to more computationally intensive methods like activation patching.
future_direction: Incorporate more diverse datasets, additional model variants, and alternative interpretability techniques.
papers.abstract: Understanding how large language models (LLMs) acquire and store factual knowledge is crucial for enhancing their interpretability and reliability. In this work, we analyze the evolution of factual knowledge representation in the OLMo-7B model by tracking the roles of its attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) over the course of pre-training. We classify these components into four roles: general, entity, relation-answer, and fact-answer specific, and examine their stability and transitions. Our results show that LLMs initially depend on broad, general-purpose components, which later specialize as training progresses. Once the model reliably predicts answers, some components are repurposed, suggesting an adaptive learning process. Notably, attention heads display the highest turnover. We also present evidence that FFNs remain more stable throughout training. Furthermore, our probing experiments reveal that location-based relations converge to high accuracy earlier in training than name-based relations, highlighting how task complexity shapes acquisition dynamics. These insights offer a mechanistic view of knowledge formation in LLMs.

papers.title: Neuron-Level Differentiation of Memorization and Generalization in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do distinct sets of neurons underlie memorization and generalization behaviors in LLMs? Can targeted neuron-level interventions at inference time steer model behavior toward memorization or generalization? Are the observed neuron-behavior associations consistent across retraining runs and transferable across different tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that memorization and generalization activate distinct neuron subsets within LLMs, and that intervening on these subsets can controllably alter model behavior, with these neuron-behavior mappings being stable across intra-task and inter-task variations.
papers.conclusion: Memorization and generalization are encoded in separable neural pathways within LLMs, enabling inference-time steering and revealing consistent functional modularity.
papers.key_findings:
Distinct neuron subsets are responsible for memorization and generalization behaviors in LLMs.
Inference-time interventions on these neurons can steer the model's behavior toward memorization or generalization.
The neuron-behavior associations are consistent across retraining runs on the same task (intra-task consistency).
Neurons identified from one task can transfer to another task to some extent (inter-task transferability).
Behavior-associated signals originate primarily in the pretrained base model rather than the LoRA adapter.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to GPT-2 and LLaMA 3.2 models, lacking validation on diverse architectures and scales.
Evaluation uses only two task types (induction-style in-context inference and arithmetic addition), not capturing the breadth of language tasks.
The operationalization of generalization is comparatively less complete than memorization, capturing only specific forms.
The inference-time intervention uses a straightforward linear neuron-shifting method, which may not be optimal.
future_direction: Broader validation on diverse architectures and scales.
Examination of more varied tasks such as QA, commonsense reasoning, or dialogue.
Development of improved neuron selection methods for higher behavioral specificity.
papers.abstract: We investigate how Large Language Models (LLMs) distinguish between memorization and generalization at the neuron level. Through carefully designed tasks, we identify distinct neuron subsets responsible for each behavior. Experiments on both a GPT-2 model trained from scratch and a pretrained LLaMA-3.2 model fine-tuned with LoRA show consistent neuron-level specialization. We further demonstrate that inference-time interventions on these neurons can steer the model's behavior toward memorization or generalization. To assess robustness, we evaluate intra-task and inter-task consistency, confirming that these neuron-behavior associations reflect generalizable patterns rather than dataset-specific artifacts. Our findings reveal modular structure in LLMs and enable controlling memorization and generalization behaviors at inference time.

papers.title: Focus Directions Make Your Language Models Pay More Attention to Relevant Contexts
papers.research_question: Why are long-context large language models (LLMs) distracted by irrelevant contexts, and can this distraction be mitigated by increasing attention to relevant contexts?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies 'contextual heads' that control overall attention in LLMs and introduces 'focus directions'—vectors added to key and query activations—that can steer these heads to pay more attention to relevant contexts, mitigating distraction in long-context tasks.
papers.conclusion: Contextual heads and focus directions provide a mechanism to understand and mitigate distraction in long-context LLMs, offering a pathway for improving model alignment by steering attention to relevant information.
papers.key_findings:
Contextual heads are a sparse set of attention heads, mostly in middle and late layers, that control the overall attention of the LLM to input tokens.
Distraction arises when contextual heads fail to allocate sufficient attention to relevant contexts; increasing attention on these heads mitigates distraction.
Focus directions, located in the key and query activation spaces of contextual heads, can be added at inference to increase attention to relevant contexts without external labels.
Applying positive focus directions (up to an optimal strength) improves task performance, while negative directions or overly strong positive directions harm performance.
Focus directions are generalizable across models and tasks, and can help mitigate poor task alignment, especially in models with inconsistent attention behavior.
papers.limitation:
Focus directions may be task-dependent; the paper does not claim to have found the 'optimal' focus direction for every task.
Applying overly strong focus directions can inadvertently heighten attention to irrelevant contexts, degrading performance.
future_direction: Exploring task-dependent focus directions and whether optimal task focus directions lead to convergent attention activation across tasks.
Using focus directions as an alternative approach for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of long-context models.
Using focus directions as a 'switch' to control the LLM's use of contextual versus internal knowledge to address knowledge conflicts.
papers.abstract: Long-context large language models (LLMs) are prone to be distracted by irrelevant contexts. The reason for distraction remains poorly understood. In this paper, we first identify the contextual heads, a special group of attention heads that control the overall attention of the LLM. Then, we demonstrate that distraction arises when contextual heads fail to allocate sufficient attention to relevant contexts and can be mitigated by increasing attention to these contexts. We further identify focus directions, located at the key and query activations of these heads, which enable them to allocate more attention to relevant contexts without explicitly specifying which context is relevant. We comprehensively evaluate the effect of focus direction on various long-context tasks and find out focus directions could help to mitigate the poor task alignment of the long-context LLMs. We believe our findings could promote further research on long-context LLM alignment.

papers.title: How do language models learn facts? Dynamics, curricula and hallucinations
papers.research_question: How do language models acquire factual knowledge during training, and what are the dynamics, the impact of data distribution, and the challenges of integrating new knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a three-phase learning process for factual recall in language models, shows how data distribution affects dynamics, and demonstrates that fine-tuning to add new knowledge is challenging due to hallucinations and corruption of existing memories.
papers.conclusion: The paper emphasizes the importance of data distribution in knowledge acquisition and suggests data scheduling strategies to accelerate training, while highlighting the difficulty of integrating new knowledge post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Language models learn factual recall in three phases: initial language understanding, a performance plateau, and then knowledge emergence.
The plateau phase corresponds to the development of attention-based recall circuits.
Imbalanced data distributions shorten the plateau but can lead to overfitting.
Hallucinations (overconfident predictions on unseen individuals) emerge simultaneously with knowledge acquisition.
Fine-tuning to incorporate new knowledge quickly corrupts existing parametric memories.
papers.limitation: The results do not rule out that other qualitative changes may occur during the plateau phase, and they do not provide any mechanistic insights regarding how models acquire individual-specific knowledge.
future_direction: Further investigation is needed to better understand the precise conditions under which data repetition can effectively reduce time spent on performance plateaus during training.
The data scheduling strategy could be dynamically adjusted based on observed plateau termination.
papers.abstract: Large language models accumulate vast knowledge during pre-training, yet the dynamics governing this acquisition remain poorly understood. This work investigates the learning dynamics of language models on a synthetic factual recall task, uncovering three key findings: First, language models learn in three phases, exhibiting a performance plateau before acquiring precise factual knowledge. Mechanistically, this plateau coincides with the formation of attention-based circuits that support recall. Second, the training data distribution significantly impacts learning dynamics, as imbalanced distributions lead to shorter plateaus. Finally, hallucinations emerge simultaneously with knowledge, and integrating new knowledge into the model through fine-tuning is challenging, as it quickly corrupts its existing parametric memories. Our results emphasize the importance of data distribution in knowledge acquisition and suggest novel data scheduling strategies to accelerate neural network training.

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the truthfulness of large language models by intervening on their activations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a minimally invasive technique that shifts activations along truthful directions in attention heads during inference to improve model truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: ITI is a promising, efficient method for improving truthfulness in LLMs, suggesting that models internally represent truth which can be elicited through activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ITI significantly improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark, e.g., increasing Alpaca's truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness that can be balanced by tuning intervention strength.
ITI is data-efficient, requiring only a few hundred examples to find truthful directions.
ITI generalizes to other question-answering benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU) with smaller improvements.
LLMs appear to have an internal representation of truth even when generating falsehoods.
papers.limitation:
ITI is not sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs and should be part of a more comprehensive approach.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness; increasing truthfulness may reduce informativeness.
future_direction: Test ITI on a wider variety of benchmarks beyond TruthfulQA.
Investigate the mechanistic understanding of what ITI does to internal representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: Slow manifolds in recurrent networks encode working memory efficiently and robustly
papers.research_question: What dynamical mechanisms encode working memory in recurrent neural networks, and what are their functional advantages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that working memory in RNNs can be efficiently and robustly encoded via slow manifolds, leading to phasic activity, as opposed to direct fixed point encoding which is persistent but fragile.
papers.conclusion: Slow manifold encoding in recurrent networks offers an efficient and robust mechanism for working memory, with implications for understanding neural circuits and artificial intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
Four distinct dynamical mechanisms emerge from training RNNs on a working memory task: direct fixed point (DFP), indirect fixed point (IFP), limit cycle (LC), and mixed encoding.
Indirect fixed point encoding uses slow manifolds to maintain memory representations, leading to phasic neuronal activity.
Indirect encoding is more efficient in terms of attractor landscape usage, requiring fewer fixed points.
Indirect encoding is forgetful over extended delays but more robust to noise compared to direct encoding.
The emergence of these mechanisms depends on initial network parameters like connectivity strength and feedback variance.
papers.limitation: The analysis is restricted to the positive quadrant of state space due to network design, leaving mirror fixed points unused.
future_direction: Investigating whether the unused mirror fixed points can enable fast learning of related tasks (meta-learning).
papers.abstract: Working memory is a cognitive function involving the storage and manipulation of latent information over brief intervals of time, thus making it crucial for context-dependent computation. Here, we use a top-down modeling approach to examine network-level mechanisms of working memory, an enigmatic issue and central topic of study in neuroscience and machine intelligence. We train thousands of recurrent neural networks on a working memory task and then perform dynamical systems analysis on the ensuing optimized networks, wherein we find that four distinct dynamical mechanisms can emerge. In particular, we show the prevalence of a mechanism in which memories are encoded along slow stable manifolds in the network state space, leading to a phasic neuronal activation profile during memory periods. In contrast to mechanisms in which memories are directly encoded at stable attractors, these networks naturally forget stimuli over time. Despite this seeming functional disadvantage, they are more efficient in terms of how they leverage their attractor landscape and paradoxically, are considerably more robust to noise. Our results provide new dynamical hypotheses regarding how working memory function is encoded in both natural and artificial neural networks.

papers.title: Do All Autoregressive Transformers Remember Facts the Same Way? A Cross-Architecture Analysis of Recall Mechanisms
papers.research_question: Do findings on factual recall mechanisms in GPT-style models generalize across different autoregressive Transformer architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that factual recall mechanisms differ across autoregressive Transformer architectures, with Qwen-based models relying more on Attention modules compared to GPT-based models which use MLP modules.
papers.conclusion: Architectural variations in autoregressive Transformers lead to different mechanisms of factual recall, emphasizing the need for architecture-aware approaches in model editing and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
In GPT-based models, MLP modules in early layers play a key role in storing factual associations.
In Qwen-based models, early Attention layers contribute more to factual recall than MLP modules.
Gini coefficient analysis shows that Attention modules in Qwen models have concentrated effects on factual recall.
Semantic similarity-based evaluation confirms the differential contributions of Attention and MLP modules across architectures.
The severing effects method has limitations in accurately reflecting the contribution of Attention modules to factual recall.
papers.limitation:
the internal mechanisms by which factual associations are recalled during inference remain insufficiently understood
how factual associations are dynamically accessed across different architectures remains unclear
the interpretation of such structural differences is limited
papers.abstract: Understanding how Transformer-based language models store and retrieve factual associations is critical for improving interpretability and enabling targeted model editing. Prior work, primarily on GPT-style models, has identified MLP modules in early layers as key contributors to factual recall. However, it remains unclear whether these findings generalize across different autoregressive architectures. To address this, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of factual recall across several models -- including GPT, LLaMA, Qwen, and DeepSeek -- analyzing where and how factual information is encoded and accessed. Consequently, we find that Qwen-based models behave differently from previous patterns: attention modules in the earliest layers contribute more to factual recall than MLP modules. Our findings suggest that even within the autoregressive Transformer family, architectural variations can lead to fundamentally different mechanisms of factual recall.

papers.title: If Attention Serves as a Cognitive Model of Human Memory Retrieval, What is the Plausible Memory Representation?
papers.research_question: Investigates whether the attention mechanism of Transformer Grammar (TG), which uniquely operates on syntactic structures as representational units, can serve as a cognitive model of human memory retrieval, using Normalized Attention Entropy (NAE) as a linking hypothesis.
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that Transformer Grammar's attention, operating on syntactic structures, better predicts human reading times than vanilla Transformer, suggesting dual memory representations in human sentence processing with attention as a general memory retrieval algorithm.
papers.conclusion: Attention can serve as the general algorithm for modeling human memory retrieval from two representational systems, and Transformer Grammar, with its syntactic structure-based attention, best captures dominant factors in human sentence processing.
papers.key_findings:
TG's NAE has stronger predictive power for reading times than Transformer's NAE.
TG's and Transformer's NAE have independent contributions to reading time prediction, suggesting they capture distinct aspects of memory retrieval.
TG's NAE captures interference effects, independent of decay effects modeled by Category Locality Theory.
TG's advantage over TG−comp indicates the importance of treating closed phrases as single representations (via COMPOSE attention) for capturing syntax-based memory retrieval.
The attention mechanism serves as a general algorithm for modeling human memory retrieval from dual representational systems (syntactic and token-based).
papers.limitation:
The NAE calculation procedure (summing across heads, handling subwords) strictly followed Oh and Schuler (2022), but alternative approaches warrant investigation.
The findings are based on the English Natural Stories corpus; generalizability to other languages and cognitive measures (e.g., gaze duration, EEG) remains to be investigated.
The use of 'perfect oracles' for syntactic structures idealizes away from local ambiguities that humans encounter during actual sentence processing.
future_direction: Incorporate more realistic elements such as parallel parsing, left-corner parsing strategies, and memory decay mechanisms to fully operate at the algorithmic level.
Investigate generalizability to different languages and other measures of cognitive load.
Explore alternative approaches to handling layers, attention heads, and subword tokens in NAE calculation.
papers.abstract: Recent work in computational psycholinguistics has revealed intriguing parallels between attention mechanisms and human memory retrieval, focusing primarily on vanilla Transformers that operate on token-level representations. However, computational psycholinguistic research has also established that syntactic structures provide compelling explanations for human sentence processing that token-level factors cannot fully account for. In this paper, we investigate whether the attention mechanism of Transformer Grammar (TG), which uniquely operates on syntactic structures as representational units, can serve as a cognitive model of human memory retrieval, using Normalized Attention Entropy (NAE) as a linking hypothesis between models and humans. Our experiments demonstrate that TG's attention achieves superior predictive power for self-paced reading times compared to vanilla Transformer's, with further analyses revealing independent contributions from both models. These findings suggest that human sentence processing involves dual memory representations -- one based on syntactic structures and another on token sequences -- with attention serving as the general memory retrieval algorithm, while highlighting the importance of incorporating syntactic structures as representational units.

papers.title: Promote, Suppress, Iterate: How Language Models Answer One-to-Many Factual Queries
papers.research_question: How do language models internally implement and integrate knowledge recall and repetition avoidance for one-to-many factual queries?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a promote-then-suppress mechanism in language models for one-to-many factual queries, where attention propagates subject information and MLPs promote answers, then attention suppresses previous answers with MLPs amplifying the suppression signal.
papers.conclusion: LMs promote all answers and then suppress previously generated ones, using attention and MLPs to integrate subject and previous answer tokens for knowledge recall and repetition avoidance.
papers.key_findings:
LMs first promote all possible answers and then suppress previously generated ones.
Attention copies subject information to the last token, and MLPs use this information to promote answers.
Previous answer tokens are used for both knowledge recall (promoting new answers) and suppression.
Attention suppresses previous answers, and MLPs amplify this suppression signal.
The last token aggregates knowledge recall and suppression information to generate distinct answers.
papers.limitation:
Low accuracy due to long-tail entities, outdated datasets, and strict exact-match evaluation.
Analysis focuses only on correct cases, not on errors or unreliable signals.
future_direction: Investigate possible redundancies in how LMs encode knowledge across multiple tokens.
Examine patterns when LMs use unreliable signals or make errors.
papers.abstract: To answer one-to-many factual queries (e.g., listing cities of a country), a language model (LM) must simultaneously recall knowledge and avoid repeating previous answers. How are these two subtasks implemented and integrated internally? Across multiple datasets, models, and prompt templates, we identify a promote-then-suppress mechanism: the model first recalls all answers, and then suppresses previously generated ones. Specifically, LMs use both the subject and previous answer tokens to perform knowledge recall, with attention propagating subject information and MLPs promoting the answers. Then, attention attends to and suppresses previous answer tokens, while MLPs amplify the suppression signal. Our mechanism is corroborated by extensive experimental evidence: in addition to using early decoding and causal tracing, we analyze how components use different tokens by introducing both Token Lens, which decodes aggregated attention updates from specified tokens, and a knockout method that analyzes changes in MLP outputs after removing attention to specified tokens. Overall, we provide new insights into how LMs' internal components interact with different input tokens to support complex factual recall. Code is available at https://github.com/Lorenayannnnn/how-lms-answer-one-to-many-factual-queries.

papers.title: Identifying Semantic Induction Heads to Understand In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether attention heads in transformers encode semantic relationships (syntactic dependencies and knowledge graph relations) and how the formation of such semantic induction heads correlates with the emergence of in-context learning abilities.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers semantic induction heads in transformers that encode semantic relationships and shows their emergence correlates with the development of in-context learning abilities.
papers.conclusion: The study of semantic induction heads advances understanding of attention head operations and provides insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in transformers encode syntactic dependencies (subj, obj, mod) and semantic relationships from knowledge graphs.
The model's ability to understand dependencies is reflected in attention heads, with some heads specializing in specific relations.
In-context learning emerges progressively in three levels: loss reduction, format compliance, and pattern discovery.
The formation of semantic induction heads coincides with the emergence of pattern discovery in ICL.
Semantic induction heads are crucial for the model's ability to perform in-context learning.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, the lack of transparency in their inference logic raises concerns about their trustworthiness. To gain a better understanding of LLMs, we conduct a detailed analysis of the operations of attention heads and aim to better understand the in-context learning of LLMs. Specifically, we investigate whether attention heads encode two types of relationships between tokens present in natural languages: the syntactic dependency parsed from sentences and the relation within knowledge graphs. We find that certain attention heads exhibit a pattern where, when attending to head tokens, they recall tail tokens and increase the output logits of those tail tokens. More crucially, the formulation of such semantic induction heads has a close correlation with the emergence of the in-context learning ability of language models. The study of semantic attention heads advances our understanding of the intricate operations of attention heads in transformers, and further provides new insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.

papers.title: Too Big to Think: Capacity, Memorization, and Generalization in Pre-Trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does model capacity affect the trade-off between memorization and generalization in pre-trained Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Small Transformer models generalize to unseen arithmetic cases but fail to memorize facts, while larger models memorize facts but fail to extrapolate; no model size achieves both when tasks are combined, indicating an inherent trade-off between memorization and generalization.
papers.conclusion: The trade-off between memorization and generalization is a structural consequence of model capacity, not just a byproduct of training dynamics. Future language model design should account for this trade-off, possibly via modular architectures that separate memorization from generalization pathways.
papers.key_findings:
The smallest model (n14) achieves perfect accuracy on held-out arithmetic cases but only 8.2% on factual recall.
Larger models (n28, n56, MLT) achieve perfect factual recall but fail on all held-out arithmetic cases.
Intermediate models show a transition from generalization to memorization as capacity increases.
When trained jointly on both tasks, no model generalizes to held-out arithmetic cases, and the smallest model's performance degrades on both tasks.
Extended training (1.5M iterations) on the arithmetic task for the large model did not lead to generalization (no grokking observed).
papers.limitation: The n14 model's generalization is shallow and does not extend to multi-digit inputs, indicating limited extrapolation rather than robust generalization.
future_direction: Explore whether these dynamics extend to real-world domains.
Investigate training strategies to better balance memorization and generalization.
Explore modular or specialized architectures that separate memorization from generalization pathways.
papers.abstract: The relationship between memorization and generalization in large language models (LLMs) remains an open area of research, with growing evidence that the two are deeply intertwined. In this work, we investigate this relationship by pre-training a series of capacity-limited Transformer models from scratch on two synthetic character-level tasks designed to separately probe generalization (via arithmetic extrapolation) and memorization (via factual recall). We observe a consistent trade-off: small models extrapolate to unseen arithmetic cases but fail to memorize facts, while larger models memorize but fail to extrapolate. An intermediate-capacity model exhibits a similar shift toward memorization. When trained on both tasks jointly, no model (regardless of size) succeeds at extrapolation. These findings suggest that pre-training may intrinsically favor one learning mode over the other. By isolating these dynamics in a controlled setting, our study offers insight into how model capacity shapes learning behavior and offers broader implications for the design and deployment of small language models.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: Beyond Memorization: The Challenge of Random Memory Access in Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether a generative language model is able to access its memory sequentially or randomly.
papers.core_contribution: Language models can sequentially access memorized content but struggle with random access; recitation and permutation techniques mitigate this challenge and improve performance in question answering.
papers.conclusion: Language models struggle with random memory access, but recitation and permutation mitigate this limitation, and recitation improves performance in open-domain question answering.
papers.key_findings:
Language models can sequentially access memorized content but encounter significant challenges in random memory access.
Recitation (loading memorized content into the context window) enables random access and improves task performance.
Permutation of sentences during training enhances random access capability.
Improving random access via recitation leads to notable gains in open-domain question answering.
The challenges and mitigations are generalizable across different model sizes and architectures (GPT-2, Qwen, Llama).
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to decoder-only language models; future research is needed for encoder-only and encoder-decoder models.
The study does not extend to models beyond 7 billion parameters due to computing resource constraints.
Controlled experiments are conducted on a text corpus of fixed size; implications on large-scale pretraining corpus are not explored.
future_direction: Extend the study to other types of language models (encoder-only, encoder-decoder).
Explore memory access patterns in larger language models beyond 7B parameters.
Investigate the findings on large-scale pretraining corpus and their implications on pretrained language models.
papers.abstract: Recent developments in Language Models (LMs) have shown their effectiveness in NLP tasks, particularly in knowledge-intensive tasks. However, the mechanisms underlying knowledge storage and memory access within their parameters remain elusive. In this paper, we investigate whether a generative LM (e.g., GPT-2) is able to access its memory sequentially or randomly. Through carefully-designed synthetic tasks, covering the scenarios of full recitation, selective recitation and grounded question answering, we reveal that LMs manage to sequentially access their memory while encountering challenges in randomly accessing memorized content. We find that techniques including recitation and permutation improve the random memory access capability of LMs. Furthermore, by applying this intervention to realistic scenarios of open-domain question answering, we validate that enhancing random access by recitation leads to notable improvements in question answering. The code to reproduce our experiments can be found at https://github.com/sail-sg/lm-random-memory-access.

papers.title: Characterizing Verbatim Short-Term Memory in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: What kind of information about the prior context can language models retrieve? Specifically, can they retrieve the exact words (verbatim) that occurred previously in a text?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers implement a working memory-like system that can flexibly retrieve individual token representations verbatim, while LSTMs maintain a coarser, rapidly-decaying semantic gist of prior context.
papers.conclusion: The introduced paradigm can illuminate the memory systems in neural language models, revealing that transformers develop detailed verbatim short-term memory while LSTMs maintain a coarse gist.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers retrieve both the identity and ordering of nouns from prior context, and this retrieval is robust to set size and intervening text length.
Transformer retrieval is learned and depends on attention mechanisms; shuffling attention weights reduces retrieval.
Transformer retrieval improves with larger training corpus and greater model depth.
LSTMs exhibit less precise retrieval, limited to list-initial tokens and short intervening texts, and are not sensitive to word order.
LSTM retrieval improves when the list is semantically coherent.
future_direction: Apply the paradigm to other transformer models (e.g., BERT, T5).
Test LSTM architectures augmented with attention or a copy-mechanism.
Perform targeted ablations of specific attention heads to pinpoint the mechanistic locus of short-term memory.
papers.abstract: When a language model is trained to predict natural language sequences, its prediction at each moment depends on a representation of prior context. What kind of information about the prior context can language models retrieve? We tested whether language models could retrieve the exact words that occurred previously in a text. In our paradigm, language models (transformers and an LSTM) processed English text in which a list of nouns occurred twice. We operationalized retrieval as the reduction in surprisal from the first to the second list. We found that the transformers retrieved both the identity and ordering of nouns from the first list. Further, the transformers' retrieval was markedly enhanced when they were trained on a larger corpus and with greater model depth. Lastly, their ability to index prior tokens was dependent on learned attention patterns. In contrast, the LSTM exhibited less precise retrieval, which was limited to list-initial tokens and to short intervening texts. The LSTM's retrieval was not sensitive to the order of nouns and it improved when the list was semantically coherent. We conclude that transformers implemented something akin to a working memory system that could flexibly retrieve individual token representations across arbitrary delays; conversely, the LSTM maintained a coarser and more rapidly-decaying semantic gist of prior tokens, weighted toward the earliest items.

papers.title: Identifying and Evaluating Inactive Heads in Pretrained LLMs
papers.research_question: How prevalent are inactive attention heads in pretrained LLMs? The paper evaluates score functions that measure different ways a head can be inactive.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces 12 score functions to identify inactive attention heads and shows that more than 12% of heads are inactive on average, and can be ablated while maintaining MMLU accuracy within 1%. It finds that measuring average head output norm is more effective than relying on attention sink patterns.
papers.conclusion: Understanding inactive attention heads requires looking beyond attention weights. The paper shows that more than 12% of heads can be zeroed out while maintaining accuracy within 1% of baseline, and average head output norm is the best signal for identifying inactive heads across model families.
papers.key_findings:
More than 12% of attention heads are inactive on average in pretrained LLMs.
Average Head Output Norm (LN) is the best score function for identifying inactive heads across model families.
Relying on attention sink patterns (Avg Weight of First Token) underestimates inactive heads by missing more than 7% on average.
Finetuning causes minimal changes in attention behavior.
Model scale has little effect on attention behavior until very large sizes.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses on single forward passes as used in log-likelihood evaluations of multiple-choice benchmarks; analyzing generation is more complex and left for future work.
The best score function (AHON (LN)) requires computing the head output itself, which prevents compute savings when skipping heads.
future_direction: Analyzing generation tasks where zeroing out heads might have cascading effects.
Developing new architectures that leverage inactive heads for efficiency, such as dynamic pruning or KV cache compression.
Discovering better score functions that allow for compute savings by not requiring head output computation.
papers.abstract: Attention is foundational to large language models (LLMs), enabling different heads to have diverse focus on relevant input tokens. However, learned behaviors like attention sinks, where the first token receives the most attention despite limited semantic importance, suggest some heads may be inactive, and point to a significant source of computational redundancy. To analyze this phenomenon, we propose a taxonomy of 13 score functions that measure different ways a head can be inactive. Thresholding these scores allows us to analyze different sets of potentially inactive attention heads. We evaluate whether identified heads are inactive through model interventions, finding that more than 12% of attention heads are inactive on average, and can be ablated in specific contexts while maintaining MMLU accuracy to within 1% of the pretrained LLM. Across 3 model families, our score functions that measure the average norm of a head's output consistently identify inactive heads that would not have been found by score functions that rely solely on attention weights. We establish that relying on a score function that measures a first token attention sink would underestimate the prevalence of inactive heads, failing to identify more than 7% of inactive heads on average. We also show how measuring score distributions can provide insights into attention behavior. For instance, we find evidence that finetuning causes little to no change in attention behavior, and that even within the same model family, large model scales present markedly different attention behaviors.

papers.title: Understanding Transformer Memorization Recall Through Idioms
papers.research_question: When does a model decide to output a memorized phrase, and how is this phrase then retrieved from memory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a methodological framework and dataset for probing memorization recall in transformers, and finds that memorized predictions involve a two-step process of candidate promotion in early layers and confidence boosting in upper layers.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our work makes a first step towards understanding memory recall, and provides a methodological basis for future studies of transformer memorization.
papers.key_findings:
