Intervening on these activations allows us to suppress memorization without degrading overall performance, enhancing evaluation integrity by ensuring metrics reflect genuine generalization. Additionally, our method supports large-scale labeling of tokens and sequences, crucial for next-generation AI models, improving training efficiency and results. Our findings contribute to model interpretability and offer practical tools for analyzing and controlling internal mechanisms in LLMs.

papers.title: Do LLMs dream of elephants (when told not to)? Latent concept association and associative memory in transformers
papers.research_question: How robust is fact retrieval in LLMs to context changes, and what does this reveal about associative memory mechanisms in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that fact retrieval in LLMs is not robust and can be hijacked by context, and proposes a synthetic latent concept association task to show transformers implement associative memory via self-attention for aggregation and the value matrix for memory retrieval.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit associative memory behavior, which makes fact retrieval non-robust, and understanding this can help develop more robust models.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are susceptible to context hijacking, where adding context that does not change factual meaning can lead to incorrect fact retrieval.
The latent concept association task models fact retrieval in transformers and shows that transformers can solve it by using self-attention to aggregate information and the value matrix as associative memory.
Theoretical analysis shows that the value matrix is crucial for associative memory and that the embedding space can exhibit a low-rank structure.
In the underparameterized regime, embedding training is necessary for good performance, and the learned embeddings have a structure that relates inner product to Hamming distance.
The attention mechanism can select relevant tokens based on latent clusters, mitigating noise.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to open-source models and may not generalize to commercial models like GPT-4.
The theoretical analysis focuses on single-layer transformers, while multi-layer transformers have more complex behaviors (e.g., induction heads).
future_direction: Extending the analysis to multi-layer transformers.
Studying more complex associative memory mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have the capacity to store and recall facts. Through experimentation with open-source models, we observe that this ability to retrieve facts can be easily manipulated by changing contexts, even without altering their factual meanings. These findings highlight that LLMs might behave like an associative memory model where certain tokens in the contexts serve as clues to retrieving facts. We mathematically explore this property by studying how transformers, the building blocks of LLMs, can complete such memory tasks. We study a simple latent concept association problem with a one-layer transformer and we show theoretically and empirically that the transformer gathers information using self-attention and uses the value matrix for associative memory.

papers.title: Cutting Off the Head Ends the Conflict: A Mechanism for Interpreting and Mitigating Knowledge Conflicts in Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the mechanism of knowledge conflicts in language models, and how can they be mitigated by precise interventions at the pivotal point?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that knowledge conflicts in language models arise from the integration of inconsistent information flows by memory heads and context heads in later layers, and proposes a parameter-free method (PH3) to mitigate conflicts by pruning these heads.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a mechanistic interpretation of knowledge conflicts in LMs and demonstrates that the proposed PH3 method can effectively mitigate these conflicts and control model behavior, showing strong generalization across models, relations, and data formats.
papers.key_findings:
FFNs in early layers enrich the semantic information of input elements, while MHAs in middle and late layers are crucial for passing information to the last token.
The last token extracts attribute information from the context subject (internal memory) and context attribute (external context) in later layers.
Some attention heads in late MHAs play opposite roles: memory heads recall knowledge from internal memory, and context heads retrieve knowledge from external context.
The pivotal point of knowledge conflict is the integration of inconsistent information flows by memory heads and context heads.
The proposed PH3 method can flexibly control LMs to use internal memory (↑44.0%) or external context (↑38.5%) by pruning conflicting attention heads without updating parameters.

papers.title: SCIURus: Shared Circuits for Interpretable Uncertainty Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do the factuality of generated responses and a model's uncertainty originate in separate or shared circuits within the model architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides strong evidence that a language model's uncertainty and the factuality of its generated answers are produced by shared circuits in the model, rather than separate ones.
papers.conclusion: The results broadly support the shared circuits hypothesis, suggesting that P(IK) probing elicits introspective, interpretable uncertainty estimates and that uncertainty quantification in LLMs may largely rely on the same circuitry used for question-answering.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing experiments show that the same model components (layers, attention heads) affect both the model's correct-token probability and the P(IK) probe's confidence estimate.
Zero-ablation experiments (both leave-one-out and COAR) across multiple models and datasets support the shared circuits hypothesis, with changes in model accuracy and probe output being highly correlated.
The P(IK) probe's uncertainty representation often remains calibrated even after interventions that damage model performance.
The shared circuits hypothesis holds across a range of models (Llama 2/3, Gemma 2) and datasets (TriviaQA, WebQuestions, MMLU, ARC, CounterFact).
Some discrepancies occur, such as when answer tokens appear in the question, where restorations can suppress model accuracy but not probe confidence.
papers.limitation:
Zero-ablation may lack specificity because zeroing out a component can severely damage general language coherence, not just task-specific information flow.
Causal tracing may miss important circuits when information flows along multiple parallel paths, as restoring a single path may not show a substantial effect.
future_direction: Analyze the mechanisms responsible for P(IK) estimates in greater detail.
Apply P(IK) probing as an interpretability tool to study phenomena like hallucination in LLMs.
Perform similar analyses on other uncertainty quantification methods, such as verbalized uncertainty.
papers.abstract: Carter Teplica, Yixin Liu, Arman Cohan, Tim G. J. Rudner. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: InversionView: A General-Purpose Method for Reading Information from Neural Activations
papers.research_question: How can we decipher the information encoded in neural activations? The paper proposes InversionView, a method to sample from the preimage of an activation to uncover the information content.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces InversionView, a method that samples from the preimage of an activation via a conditional decoder to uncover the information encoded in neural activations and understand model algorithms.
papers.conclusion: InversionView is a general-purpose method that effectively deciphers information in neural activations, enabling better understanding of model algorithms and simplifying interpretability workflows.
papers.key_findings:
InversionView can reveal both basic and complex information in activations, such as token counts and relative positions.
InversionView simplifies interpretability workflows, agreeing with prior circuit findings in GPT-2 small.
InversionView enabled the first fully verified circuit for a 3-digit addition model.
InversionView scales to larger models like GPT-2 for factual recall.
papers.limitation:
Training a decoder requires a dataset of activations and can be computationally expensive.
The decoder may not perfectly capture the preimage, leading to potential biases in the generated samples.
The method is currently limited to discrete sequences (text).
future_direction: Extend InversionView to continuous domains.
Improve decoder efficiency.
Automate interpretation using LLMs.
papers.abstract: The inner workings of neural networks can be better understood if we can fully decipher the information encoded in neural activations. In this paper, we argue that this information is embodied by the subset of inputs that give rise to similar activations. We propose InversionView, which allows us to practically inspect this subset by sampling from a trained decoder model conditioned on activations. This helps uncover the information content of activation vectors, and facilitates understanding of the algorithms implemented by transformer models. We present four case studies where we investigate models ranging from small transformers to GPT-2. In these studies, we show that InversionView can reveal clear information contained in activations, including basic information about tokens appearing in the context, as well as more complex information, such as the count of certain tokens, their relative positions, and abstract knowledge about the subject. We also provide causally verified circuits to confirm the decoded information.

papers.title: Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative circuits of components such as attention heads and MLPs, and how can these circuits be used to analyze model behaviors and knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces knowledge circuits as a method to uncover how transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative components, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing knowledge editing and model behaviors like hallucinations and in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge circuits provide a valuable framework for understanding how transformers store and express knowledge, and can inform the design of better knowledge editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge circuits effectively capture knowledge representations, maintaining over 70% of original performance with less than 10% of the graph.
Knowledge is aggregated in early-to-middle layers and enhanced in later layers.
Special components like mover heads and relation heads are critical for information transfer and relational capture.
ROME editing incorporates information at the edited layer, while fine-tuning directly writes knowledge and dominates predictions.
Hallucinations occur when the circuit lacks effective mover heads or they select incorrect information.
papers.limitation:
Coarse granularity of circuits, not capturing fine-grained neuron-level behavior.
Logit lens method may have discrepancies between middle layers and output unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Finer-grained circuit analysis at the neuron level.
Developing more robust techniques to map intermediate representations to outputs (e.g., Attention Lens).
Investigating activation mechanisms of reused heads and polysemanticity.
papers.abstract: The remarkable capabilities of modern large language models are rooted in their vast repositories of knowledge encoded within their parameters, enabling them to perceive the world and engage in reasoning. The inner workings of how these models store knowledge have long been a subject of intense interest and investigation among researchers. To date, most studies have concentrated on isolated components within these models, such as the Multilayer Perceptrons and attention head. In this paper, we delve into the computation graph of the language model to uncover the knowledge circuits that are instrumental in articulating specific knowledge. The experiments, conducted with GPT2 and TinyLLAMA, have allowed us to observe how certain information heads, relation heads, and Multilayer Perceptrons collaboratively encode knowledge within the model. Moreover, we evaluate the impact of current knowledge editing techniques on these knowledge circuits, providing deeper insights into the functioning and constraints of these editing methodologies. Finally, we utilize knowledge circuits to analyze and interpret language model behaviors such as hallucinations and in-context learning. We believe the knowledge circuits hold potential for advancing our understanding of Transformers and guiding the improved design of knowledge editing. Code and data are available in https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Exploiting Attention to Reveal Shortcomings in Memory Models
papers.research_question: How does attention analysis explain the contradictory performance of a memory network model on theory-of-mind question-answering tasks?
papers.core_contribution: By analyzing attention patterns, the paper explains why a memory network model fails on first-order belief questions but succeeds on second-order ones, linking success to task classification.
papers.conclusion: Attention analysis reveals shortcomings in memory models, and performance can be explained by how well the model classifies task types.
papers.key_findings:
The model is successful on second-order belief questions but not on first-order ones.
Attention patterns for second-order questions show sensitivity to task-relevant sentences like 'exited', aiding classification.
For first-order questions, attention is not sensitive to task type, leading to failures.
Equating success to task classification explains test-time failures and generalization.
With a modified dataset where answers are consistent, models succeed on first-order questions.
papers.abstract: The decision making processes of deep networks are difficult to understand and while their accuracy often improves with increased architectural complexity, so too does their opacity. Practical use of machine learning models, especially for question and answering applications, demands a system that is interpretable. We analyze the attention of a memory network model to reconcile contradictory performance on a challenging questionanswering dataset that is inspired by theoryof-mind experiments. We equate success on questions to task classification, which explains not only test-time failures but also how well the model generalizes to new training conditions.

papers.title: Emergence of Episodic Memory in Transformers: Characterizing Changes in Temporal Structure of Attention Scores During Training
papers.research_question: How do temporal biases (like contiguity, primacy, recency) emerge in attention heads and transformer outputs during training, and how do they relate to human episodic memory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers develop temporal biases (contiguity, primacy, recency) in attention heads during training, similar to human episodic memory, and that induction heads are crucial for the contiguity effect.
papers.conclusion: Overall, we showed that tools from cognitive science can be used to better understand learning in transformers, providing valuable insights into the emergence of temporal structure during in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Temporal contiguity, primacy, and recency effects emerge in attention heads during training.
Induction heads are the driving force behind the contiguity effect, and ablating them eliminates the effect in transformer outputs.
The magnitude of positional encoding influences the strength of recency and contiguity effects.
Temporal effects are consistent across model sizes (GPT-2 small and medium).
The time constants for contiguity are short (2-4 lags), indicating limited temporal context retrieval.
papers.limitation: The study uses relatively small models, and methodological differences prevent direct parallels with human memory.
papers.abstract: We investigate in-context temporal biases in attention heads and transformer outputs. Using cognitive science methodologies, we analyze attention scores and outputs of the GPT-2 models of varying sizes. Across attention heads, we observe effects characteristic of human episodic memory, including temporal contiguity, primacy and recency. Transformer outputs demonstrate a tendency toward in-context serial recall. Importantly, this effect is eliminated after the ablation of the induction heads, which are the driving force behind the contiguity effect. Our findings offer insights into how transformers organize information temporally during in-context learning, shedding light on their similarities and differences with human memory and learning.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Acquire New Knowledge? A Knowledge Circuits Perspective on Continual Pre-Training
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) structurally embed and acquire new knowledge during continual pre-training, from the perspective of knowledge circuit evolution?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes the evolution of knowledge circuits during continual pre-training, revealing that new knowledge acquisition is influenced by relevance to existing knowledge, follows a biphasic (formation then optimization) pattern, and exhibits a deep-to-shallow component evolution.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance the theoretical understanding of new knowledge acquisition mechanisms in LLMs and provide potential implications for improving continual pre-training strategies to enhance model performance.
papers.key_findings:
The acquisition of new knowledge is significantly influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge, with relevant new knowledge being integrated more efficiently than completely new knowledge.
The evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization, each marked by unique structural and behavioral characteristics.
The evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern, where mid-to-deeper layers first develop the extraction function, and later, lower layers enrich their knowledge representations.
The performance of knowledge circuits is positively correlated with knowledge frequency, with low-frequency knowledge circuits suffering from insufficient representations rather than fundamental capacity limitations.
The state of knowledge circuits could serve as a valuable tracking status for the continual pre-training process, enabling more informed adjustments to training.
future_direction: Utilizing data curriculums in continual pre-training to mimic the structure of the original corpus for more efficient integration.
Using the state of knowledge circuits as a tracking status to enable informed adjustments to training methods or data in response to different phases.
Further investigation into knowledge capacity scaling laws and their impact on model behavior during continual pre-training.
papers.abstract: Despite exceptional capabilities in knowledge-intensive tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) face a critical gap in understanding how they internalize new knowledge, particularly how to structurally embed acquired knowledge in their neural computations. We address this issue through the lens of knowledge circuit evolution, identifying computational subgraphs that facilitate knowledge storage and processing. Our systematic analysis of circuit evolution throughout continual pre-training reveals several key findings: (1) the acquisition of new knowledge is influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge; (2) the evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization; (3) the evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern. These insights not only advance our theoretical understanding of the mechanisms of new knowledge acquisition in LLMs, but also provide potential implications for improving continual pre-training strategies to enhance model performance. Code and data will be available at https://github.com/zjunlp/DynamicKnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Navigating the Dual Facets: A Comprehensive Evaluation of Sequential Memory Editing in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does sequential memory editing affect the general capabilities of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Parameter-modifying memory editing methods degrade LLM performance after sequential edits, while parameter-preserving methods maintain capabilities but struggle with generalization.
papers.conclusion: Parameter-modifying ME methods systematically degrade LLM performance, while GRACE maintains capabilities but lacks generalization; editing strategies can mitigate but not fully overcome damage.
papers.key_findings:
Parameter-modifying ME methods consistently degrade performance across all tasks after a few sequential edits.
Parameter-preserving ME method GRACE maintains LLM capabilities but has low generalization for edited knowledge.
Increasing model size, instruction tuning, editing deeper layers, and batch size mitigate damage but do not eliminate it.
Parameter changes after editing cause performance degradation due to increased deviation from original parameters.
In-context learning capability is maintained when editing shallow or deep layers, but damaged for middle layers.
papers.limitation:
Experiments on parameter-preserving ME methods are not exhaustive.
Incomplete explanation of why LLMs maintain in-context learning capabilities after editing.
future_direction: Further experiments on parameter-preserving ME methods
Explaining the maintenance of in-context learning capabilities after editing
papers.abstract: Memory Editing (ME) has emerged as an efficient method to modify erroneous facts or inject new facts into Large Language Models (LLMs). Two mainstream ME methods exist: parameter-modifying ME and parameter-preserving ME (integrating extra modules while preserving original parameters). Regrettably, previous studies on ME evaluation have two critical limitations: (i) evaluating LLMs with single edit only, neglecting the need for continuous editing, and (ii) evaluations focusing solely on basic factual triples, overlooking broader LLM capabilities like logical reasoning and reading understanding. This study addresses these limitations with contributions threefold: (i) We explore how ME affects a wide range of fundamental capabilities of LLMs under sequential editing. Experimental results reveal an intriguing phenomenon: Most parameter-modifying ME consistently degrade performance across all tasks after a few sequential edits. In contrast, parameter-preserving ME effectively maintains LLMs' fundamental capabilities but struggles to accurately recall edited knowledge presented in a different format. (ii) We extend our evaluation to different editing settings, such as layers to edit, model size, instruction tuning, etc. Experimental findings indicate several strategies that can potentially mitigate the adverse effects of ME. (iii) We further explain why parameter-modifying ME damages LLMs from three dimensions: parameter changes after editing, language modeling capability, and the in-context learning capability. Our in-depth study advocates more careful use of ME in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Shapley Head Pruning: Identifying and Removing Interference in Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: How can interference in multilingual transformers be reduced by identifying and pruning language-specific attention heads?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Shapley Head Pruning, a method to identify and remove language-specific attention heads in multilingual transformers, reducing interference and improving cross-lingual performance without adding parameters.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that Shapley Head Pruning effectively identifies and removes interfering attention heads, improving cross-lingual performance and providing insights into language-specific components.
papers.key_findings:
Attention Head Shapley Values exhibit language affinity, with some heads being language-specific and others language-agnostic.
Pruning attention heads with negative Shapley Values improves accuracy on XNLI and UDPOS tasks, with gains up to 24.7%.
Zero-shot pruning using Shapley Values from English can benefit other languages, but not all, indicating transferability.
Language-agnostic attention heads match synonyms across sentences, while language-specific heads have varied behavior.
The method outperforms random pruning and gradient-based baselines in iterative pruning evaluations.
papers.limitation:
Computational cost of Shapley Values is high compared to gradient-based methods.
Reliance on attention visualization for analysis, which may not be a sound analytical tool.
future_direction: Systematically understand relationships between linguistic features, training data volume, and language-specificity of attention heads.
Reduce cross-lingual interference during pre-training, such as pruning during pretraining or utilizing sparsely activated networks.
papers.abstract: Multilingual transformer-based models demonstrate remarkable zero and few-shot transfer across languages by learning and reusing language-agnostic features. However, as a fixed-size model acquires more languages, its performance across all languages degrades, a phenomenon termed interference. Often attributed to limited model capacity, interference is commonly addressed by adding additional parameters despite evidence that transformer-based models are overparameterized. In this work, we show that it is possible to reduce interference by instead identifying and pruning language-specific parameters. First, we use Shapley Values, a credit allocation metric from coalitional game theory, to identify attention heads that introduce interference. Then, we show that removing identified attention heads from a fixed model improves performance for a target language on both sentence classification and structural prediction, seeing gains as large as 24.7\%. Finally, we provide insights on language-agnostic and language-specific attention heads using attention visualization.

papers.title: Humans and language models diverge when predicting repeating text
papers.research_question: Does the similarity between human and language model next-word prediction accuracy reflect similar memory mechanisms? The paper investigates this by testing a scenario with repeating text spans where memory plays a role.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that human and language model next-word predictions diverge when memory is involved, and identifies specific attention heads responsible. It then demonstrates that adding a power-law recency bias to these heads makes the model's behavior more human-like.
papers.conclusion: Human and LM next-word prediction diverge when memory is involved, and adding a recency bias to attention heads can make the model more human-like, though at the cost of increased perplexity.
papers.key_findings:
Human and GPT-2 predictions are strongly aligned in the first presentation of a text span, but diverge in later presentations when memory plays a role.
The divergence is traced to specific attention heads in layer 6 that exhibit induction behavior, copying from previous repetitions.
Adding a learned power-law recency bias to attention heads reduces the model's superhuman recall and improves alignment with human predictions on repeated spans.
The intervention increases model perplexity on non-repeating text, indicating that the model's superior next-word prediction partly stems from its superhuman memory.
The optimization generalizes across stimuli and within stimuli to held-out prompts.
papers.limitation: The intervention increases model perplexity on non-repeating text, indicating a trade-off between human-like memory and general next-word prediction performance.
future_direction: Describe change in model states during repeated presentations, linking to in-context learning.
Use the model to learn more about human memory.
Develop alternate attention mechanisms for efficiency.
papers.abstract: Language models that are trained on the next-word prediction task have been shown to accurately model human behavior in word prediction and reading speed. In contrast with these findings, we present a scenario in which the performance of humans and LMs diverges. We collected a dataset of human next-word predictions for five stimuli that are formed by repeating spans of text. Human and GPT-2 LM predictions are strongly aligned in the first presentation of a text span, but their performance quickly diverges when memory (or in-context learning) begins to play a role. We traced the cause of this divergence to specific attention heads in a middle layer. Adding a power-law recency bias to these attention heads yielded a model that performs much more similarly to humans. We hope that this scenario will spur future work in bringing LMs closer to human behavior.

papers.title: Paying Attention to Facts: Quantifying the Knowledge Capacity of Attention Layers
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the knowledge capacity of attention layers in transformers from a linear-algebraic perspective, and what are the roles of the value-output and query-key weights in factual recall?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a linear-algebraic framework to quantify the knowledge capacity of attention layers, showing that the value-output weights are more critical for capacity than query-key weights, and that argmax and softmax can distort rank, leading to the proposal of softmax≥τ for evaluation.
papers.conclusion: A tensor-theoretic approach provides insights into the additive motif of factual recall in attention layers, highlighting the crucial role of value-output weights and the challenges of interpreting even simple models.
papers.key_findings:
The rank of a database tensor provides an upper bound on the number of facts that can be stored.
The capacity of an attention layer depends more on the value-output dimension (d_head,vo) than the query-key dimension (d_head,qk).
Argmax and softmax can significantly increase the effective rank of the model's output, allowing small models to memorize databases with higher rank.
Using softmax with a threshold τ (e.g., τ=0.95) reduces the rank distortion and provides a more reliable measure of memorization capacity.
It is possible to increase layer capacity without increasing parameters by increasing d_head,vo at the expense of d_head,qk.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to single-layer attention-only models without layer norms, biases, positional embeddings, or MLP layers.
Experiments are on small toy models and databases; it remains to be seen if results hold for larger models.
future_direction: Generalizing to n-gram statistics and deriving new rank bounds.
Studying the effect of softmax on rank in more realistic settings.
Investigating the impact of adding layer norms, biases, positional embeddings, MLP layers, and multiple layers.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the ability of single-layer attention-only transformers (i.e. attention layers) to memorize facts contained in databases from a linear-algebraic perspective. We associate with each database a 3-tensor, propose the rank of this tensor as a measure of the size of the database, and provide bounds on the rank in terms of properties of the database. We also define a 3-tensor corresponding to an attention layer, and empirically demonstrate the relationship between its rank and database rank on a dataset of toy models and random databases. By highlighting the roles played by the value-output and query-key weights, and the effects of argmax and softmax on rank, our results shed light on the `additive motif' of factual recall in transformers, while also suggesting a way of increasing layer capacity without increasing the number of parameters.

papers.title: Neural flip-flops I: Short-term memory
papers.research_question: How can neurons be connected to form flip-flops, the basic building blocks for sequential logic and short-term memory, and can such neural flip-flops explain known phenomena and make testable predictions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes neural flip-flops (NFFs) as explicit, dynamic models for short-term memory, showing they can generate known neural activity phenomena and predict eight unknown testable phenomena.
papers.conclusion: Neural flip-flops are plausible, simple, and fast mechanisms for short-term memory, consistent with observed neural activity and capable of generating known and testable unknown phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Neural flip-flops (NFFs) composed of two or four neurons can function as sequential logic elements for storing one bit of information.
One output neuron of an NFF exhibits the seven known characteristics of neuron firing during short-term memory: baseline activity, stimulus-triggered high firing, persistence after stimulus, maintenance during recall, return to baseline after test, and cessation or absence of firing in error trials.
The pair of output neurons in an NFF predict eight unknown phenomena, including complementary outputs, reciprocal inhibitory inputs, close proximity, noise-reducing responses, and specific temporal order during state changes.
The NFF designs are derived from standard electronic flip-flop designs by moving negation symbols, transforming the logic of each component to a function implementable by a single neuron.
NFFs, together with a decoder from prior work, suggest a resolution to the controversy over whether short-term memory relies on persistent firing or brief bursts.
future_direction: Test the eight predicted unknown phenomena using the same methods that discovered the initial seven.
Construct the proposed neural networks with actual neurons and test their predicted behavior.
papers.abstract: The networks proposed here show how neurons can be connected to form flip-flops, the basic building blocks in sequential logic systems. The novel neural flip-flops (NFFs) are explicit, dynamic, and can generate known phenomena of short-term memory. For each network design, all neurons, connections, and types of synapses are shown explicitly. The neurons' operation depends only on explicitly stated, minimal properties of excitement and inhibition. This operation is dynamic in the sense that the level of neuron activity is the only cellular change, making the NFFs' operation consistent with the speed of most brain functions. Memory tests have shown that certain neurons fire continuously at a high frequency while information is held in short-term memory. These neurons exhibit seven characteristics associated with memory formation, retention, retrieval, termination, and errors. One of the neurons in each of the NFFs produces all of the characteristics. This neuron and a second neighboring neuron together predict eight unknown phenomena. These predictions can be tested by the same methods that led to the discovery of the first seven phenomena. NFFs, together with a decoder from a previous paper, suggest a resolution to the longstanding controversy of whether short-term memory depends on neurons firing persistently or in brief, coordinated bursts. Two novel NFFs are composed of two and four neurons. Their designs follow directly from a standard electronic flip-flop design by moving each negation symbol from one end of the connection to the other. This does not affect the logic of the network, but it changes the logic of each component to a logic function that can be implemented by a single neuron. This transformation is reversible and is apparently new to engineering as well as neuroscience.

papers.title: Where Knowledge Collides: A Mechanistic Study of Intra-Memory Knowledge Conflict in Language Models
papers.research_question: Which internal components of language models are responsible for encoding conflicting knowledge from pre-training data, and can noisy or incorrect information be selectively suppressed during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a mechanistic interpretability framework to localize and intervene on conflicting knowledge encoded in language models, showing that attention components in later layers play a key role in encoding and resolving such conflicts.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a mechanistic interpretability framework to study intra-memory knowledge conflict, demonstrating that logit inspection, activation patching, and cross-model patching can localize and intervene on conflicting internal representations at inference time.
papers.key_findings:
Conflicting training data reduces model confidence and introduces confusion in later layers.
Attention components in later layers dominate in shaping factual responses and encoding conflicting knowledge.
Activation patching can steer model generation toward accurate outputs, with success rates varying across models (up to 22% for GPT-2 XL and 70% for Qwen3-4B).
Cross-model activation patching (CMAP) improves steering success and reduces noise compared to standard activation patching, especially for certain conflict attributes.
Findings generalize across different model architectures (GPT-2 XL and Qwen3-4B), though intervention effectiveness varies.
papers.limitation:
Limited set of conflict types and restriction to a 1:1 ratio of conflicting information per entity.
Results are presented on a limited set of model architectures (GPT-2 XL and Qwen3-4B).
The underlying factors that drive the model's preference for one conflicting fact over another are not analyzed.
future_direction: Extend these methods to knowledge editing and robust information tracing across prompts and model variants.
Include more conflict types and multiple conflicting information per entity.
Evaluate across additional model families.
papers.abstract: In language models (LMs), intra-memory knowledge conflict largely arises when inconsistent information about the same event is encoded within the model's parametric knowledge. While prior work has primarily focused on resolving conflicts between a model's internal knowledge and external resources through approaches such as fine-tuning or knowledge editing, the problem of localizing conflicts that originate during pre-training within the model's internal representations remain unexplored. In this work, we design a framework based on mechanistic interpretability methods to identify where and how conflicting knowledge from the pre-training data is encoded within LMs. Our findings contribute to a growing body of evidence that specific internal components of a language model are responsible for encoding conflicting knowledge from pre-training, and we demonstrate how mechanistic interpretability methods can be leveraged to causally intervene in and control conflicting knowledge at inference time.

papers.title: Reason to Rote: Rethinking Memorization in Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize label noise, and why does such memorization not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Memorization of noisy labels in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, with memories stored via distributed encoding and outlier heuristics in neurons.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that memorization of label noise builds on existing reasoning mechanisms, using distributed encoding and outlier heuristics, explaining the phenomenon of benign memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Models first learn to generalize on noisy training instances (predicting correct labels) before memorizing the noisy labels.
Even when producing memorized noisy labels, models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs corresponding to the correct labels.
Memorization and generalization circuits substantially overlap, indicating memorization builds on existing generalization mechanisms.
Memorization uses distributed encoding across multiple input tokens and intermediate results rather than a simple lookup.
In the FDA task, memorization occurs via 'outlier heuristics' where higher-layer MLP neurons slightly shift their activation patterns to fit noisy labels.
papers.limitation:
Focus on relatively small language models; larger models might exhibit different behaviors.
Models trained from scratch, so influence of pretraining data is not considered.
Examination of implicit reasoning without explicit solution steps; not studying models with explicit chain-of-thought.
future_direction: Study memorization in larger models
Investigate effect of pretraining on memorization and reasoning
Study memorization in models with explicit chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models readily memorize arbitrary training instances, such as label noise, yet they perform strikingly well on reasoning tasks. In this work, we investigate how language models memorize label noise, and why such memorization in many cases does not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities. Using two controllable synthetic reasoning datasets with noisy labels, four-digit addition (FDA) and two-hop relational reasoning (THR), we discover a reliance of memorization on generalizable reasoning mechanisms: models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs even when retrieving memorized noisy labels, and intervening reasoning adversely affects memorization. We further show that memorization operates through distributed encoding, i.e., aggregating various inputs and intermediate results, rather than building a look-up mechanism from inputs to noisy labels. Moreover, our FDA case study reveals memorization occurs via outlier heuristics, where existing neuron activation patterns are slightly shifted to fit noisy labels. Together, our findings suggest that memorization of label noise in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, shedding lights on the intriguing phenomenon of benign memorization.

papers.title: Talking Heads: Understanding Inter-layer Communication in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How is information represented and routed between layers in transformer language models, specifically through low-rank communication channels?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LMs use low-rank subspaces (communication channels) in the residual stream to pass information between layers; these channels can be identified via SVD of weight matrices and are causally important for model behaviors.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn intricately structured representations through pretraining, and the discovered communication channels provide a mechanistic explanation for some prompt sensitivities, enabling improved model performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer LMs use low-rank (1D or 2D) subspaces in the residual stream for inter-layer communication.
These communication channels can be identified by applying SVD to weight matrices (OV and QK) and computing composition scores on the rank-1 components.
The identified channels are causally important for model behaviors, such as inhibition in the IOI task.
The model's sensitivity to item order in a list (Laundry List task) is explained by the limited capacity of these low-rank channels.
Model editing (zeroing or scaling components) based on these channels can significantly improve performance on the Laundry List task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not work for key composition (Appendix B).
Analysis is limited to two small models (GPT-2 small and Pythia 160m).
Difficulty in controlling all variables in the available data (Section 7).
future_direction: Future work in static weight analysis more generally.
More rigorous analysis of interactions between specific heads (e.g., 8.3 and 9.9).
Extending the method to analyze more complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: Although it is known that transformer language models (LMs) pass features from early layers to later layers, it is not well understood how this information is represented and routed by the model. We analyze a mechanism used in two LMs to selectively inhibit items in a context in one task, and find that it underlies a commonly used abstraction across many context-retrieval behaviors. Specifically, we find that models write into low-rank subspaces of the residual stream to represent features which are then read out by later layers, forming low-rank communication channels (Elhage et al., 2021) between layers. A particular 3D subspace in model activations in GPT-2 can be traversed to positionally index items in lists, and we show that this mechanism can explain an otherwise arbitrary-seeming sensitivity of the model to the order of items in the prompt. That is, the model has trouble copying the correct information from context when many items ``crowd" this limited space. By decomposing attention heads with the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that previously described interactions between heads separated by one or more layers can be predicted via analysis of their weight matrices alone. We show that it is possible to manipulate the internal model representations as well as edit model weights based on the mechanism we discover in order to significantly improve performance on our synthetic Laundry List task, which requires recall from a list, often improving task accuracy by over 20%. Our analysis reveals a surprisingly intricate interpretable structure learned from language model pretraining, and helps us understand why sophisticated LMs sometimes fail in simple domains, facilitating future analysis of more complex behaviors.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in Mamba
papers.research_question: Does factual recall in the Mamba state space model exhibit locality similar to the patterns observed in autoregressive transformer language models?
papers.core_contribution: Despite architectural differences, Mamba exhibits similar localization patterns for factual recall as transformers, and many interpretability methods developed for transformers can be adapted to Mamba.
papers.conclusion: Many interpretability methods from transformers can be adapted to Mamba, and factual recall in Mamba shows similar localization patterns, indicating architectural similarities in how different models store and recall facts.
papers.key_findings:
Activation patching in Mamba reveals high causal effects at early-middle layers (subject last token) and later layers (prompt last token), similar to transformers.
ROME editing can successfully insert facts in Mamba by modifying projection matrices, with Wo being the most effective.
The linearity of relation decoding (LRE) in Mamba is similar to transformers, with some relations being more linearly decodable than others.
Adapted attention knockout experiments show that Mamba propagates relation information in early layers and subject information in middle layers, similar to information flow in transformers.
There is a separation of roles between early-mid and later layers in Mamba for factual recall, analogous to findings in transformers.
papers.limitation: Performing attention knockout in Mamba is challenging due to the Conv+SSM operation, making it difficult to block specific edges like in transformers.
papers.abstract: We investigate the mechanisms of factual recall in the Mamba state space model. Our work is inspired by previous findings in autoregressive transformer language models suggesting that their knowledge recall is localized to particular modules at specific token locations; we therefore ask whether factual recall in Mamba can be similarly localized. To investigate this, we conduct four lines of experiments on Mamba. First, we apply causal tracing or interchange interventions to localize key components inside Mamba that are responsible for recalling facts, revealing that specific components within middle layers show strong causal effects at the last token of the subject, while the causal effect of intervening on later layers is most pronounced at the last token of the prompt, matching previous findings on autoregressive transformers. Second, we show that rank-one model editing methods can successfully insert facts at specific locations, again resembling findings on transformer LMs. Third, we examine the linearity of Mamba's representations of factual relations. Finally we adapt attention-knockout techniques to Mamba in order to dissect information flow during factual recall. We compare Mamba directly to a similar-sized autoregressive transformer LM and conclude that despite significant differences in architectural approach, when it comes to factual recall, the two architectures share many similarities.

papers.title: The Atlas of In-Context Learning: How Attention Heads Shape In-Context Retrieval Augmentation
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in large language models facilitate in-context retrieval augmentation for question answering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an attribution-based method to identify and categorize attention heads in LLMs into in-context and parametric heads, revealing their specialized roles in instruction comprehension and knowledge retrieval during in-context retrieval augmentation.
papers.conclusion: The work sheds light on the mechanism of in-context retrieval augmentation by mapping the functional roles of attention heads, paving the way for more transparent and trustworthy retrieval-augmented language models.
papers.key_findings:
An attribution-based method can reliably identify in-context heads (which process prompt information) and parametric heads (which store relational knowledge).
In-context heads specialize into task heads for instruction comprehension and retrieval heads for copying answers from context.
Function vectors extracted from these heads or modifications to their attention weights can induce specific, targeted functions and influence answer generation.
Ablation of identified heads causally affects model performance in open-book and closed-book question answering settings.
Retrieval heads can be used to trace the source of knowledge used during inference, providing a step towards transparent retrieval-augmented generation.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to a few models and datasets, and the analysis focuses on a specific task (question answering).
The proposed source tracking probe is preliminary and may not be perfect.
future_direction: Extend the approach to other tasks and models.
Improve the source tracking mechanism for retrieval-augmented generation.
Explore the interaction between attention heads more deeply.
papers.abstract: Large language models are able to exploit in-context learning to access external knowledge beyond their training data through retrieval-augmentation. While promising, its inner workings remain unclear. In this work, we shed light on the mechanism of in-context retrieval augmentation for question answering by viewing a prompt as a composition of informational components. We propose an attribution-based method to identify specialized attention heads, revealing in-context heads that comprehend instructions and retrieve relevant contextual information, and parametric heads that store entities' relational knowledge. To better understand their roles, we extract function vectors and modify their attention weights to show how they can influence the answer generation process. Finally, we leverage the gained insights to trace the sources of knowledge used during inference, paving the way towards more safe and transparent language models.

papers.title: Copy Suppression: Comprehensively Understanding a Motif in Language Model Attention Heads
papers.research_question: What is the copy suppression motif in language model attention heads, and how does it explain the behavior of negative heads like L10H7 in GPT-2 Small?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces and comprehensively analyzes the copy suppression motif in language model attention heads, showing it explains 76.9% of L10H7's behavior in GPT-2 Small and plays a role in self-repair.
papers.conclusion: Copy suppression is a fundamental motif in language model attention heads that explains negative head behavior and contributes to self-repair, with implications for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Copy suppression is a major role of negative attention heads like L10H7 in GPT-2 Small, explaining 76.9% of its behavior on OpenWebText.
The copy suppression mechanism involves three steps: naive copying by earlier components, attention to the previous instance, and suppression via writing against the unembedding.
Copy suppression improves model calibration by reducing overconfidence in incorrect copies.
Copy suppression is a form of self-repair, explaining 39% of self-repair in the IOI task after ablating name mover heads.
Copy suppression heads exist across model scales and architectures (e.g., Pythia-6B, Llama-2).
papers.limitation:
The idealized QK circuit analysis does not completely faithfully represent L10H7's real functioning.
The explanation does not account for when or how much copy suppression is activated in different contexts.
Using KL divergence as an ablation metric has limitations.
future_direction: Probe self-repair further.

papers.title: Editing Conceptual Knowledge for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs possess the capability to modify concepts (conceptual knowledge) and how to evaluate such modifications.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the task of conceptual knowledge editing for LLMs, constructs a benchmark dataset ConceptEdit, and establishes a suite of evaluation metrics including Instance Change and Concept Consistency.
papers.conclusion: Concept editing is a challenging task for LLMs, and existing editing methods have limitations in modifying conceptual knowledge without distorting related instances. This work provides a benchmark and metrics to inspire further research.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods (FT, ROME, MEMIT, PROMPT) can achieve high reliability in modifying concept-level definitions in LLMs.
These methods perform poorly on concept-specific metrics like Instance Change and Concept Consistency, indicating they distort related instance knowledge.
There is a gap between reliability (token-level accuracy) and concept consistency (semantic similarity of generated definitions).
Concept editing is easier when the replacement definition comes from the same superclass (intra module) compared to a different superclass (inter module).
Causal tracing reveals that conceptual knowledge is stored differently from instance knowledge, with attention mechanisms in earlier layers playing a key role.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are limited to models up to 7B parameters; larger models may exhibit different behaviors.
The generalization of edited concepts to unseen instances or related concepts is not fully explored.
The mechanisms of how LLMs learn and represent concepts and concept hierarchies are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring concept editing in larger-scale language models.
Improving the generalization of edited concepts to related knowledge.
Studying the mechanisms of concept learning and representation in LLMs.

papers.title: Differentiation and Specialization of Attention Heads via the Refined Local Learning Coefficient
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in a transformer language model differentiate and specialize during training, as revealed by refined local learning coefficients?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces refined local learning coefficients (rLLCs) as a principled, quantitative toolkit for developmental interpretability, revealing how attention heads differentiate and specialize during training and enabling the discovery of a novel multigram circuit.
papers.conclusion: Refined local learning coefficients provide a powerful toolkit for developmental interpretability, revealing the interplay between data distributional structure, loss landscape geometry, learning dynamics, and the resulting computational structure in neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Weight-refined LLCs (wrLLCs) reveal how attention heads differentiate into distinct functional types (e.g., induction heads, multigram heads) over the course of training.
Data-refined LLCs (drLLCs) show how heads specialize to different data distributions, such as one induction head specializing more to code.
The combination of refined LLCs leads to the identification of a novel multigram circuit involving coordination between layer 0 and layer 1 multigram heads.
The developmental perspective (evolution over time) is crucial for understanding the emergence of internal structure; point estimates at the end of training are insufficient.
Refined LLCs provide a quantitative link between data distributional structure, geometric properties of the loss landscape, learning dynamics, and emergent computational structures.
papers.limitation:
The justification of the LLC estimator presumes that w* is a local minima of the population loss, but there is no clear way to ascertain this in practice, and estimates are often performed during training where this is unlikely.
The ground truth LLC is unknown, so the accuracy of estimated LLC values cannot be guaranteed, though there is reason to believe the ordinality is correct.
future_direction: Establishing the correspondence between data distributional structure, geometric properties of the loss landscape, learning dynamics, and emergent computational structures in neural networks.
papers.abstract: We introduce refined variants of the Local Learning Coefficient (LLC), a measure of model complexity grounded in singular learning theory, to study the development of internal structure in transformer language models during training. By applying these \textit{refined LLCs} (rLLCs) to individual components of a two-layer attention-only transformer, we gain novel insights into the progressive differentiation and specialization of attention heads. Our methodology reveals how attention heads differentiate into distinct functional roles over the course of training, analyzes the types of data these heads specialize to process, and discovers a previously unidentified multigram circuit. These findings demonstrate that rLLCs provide a principled, quantitative toolkit for \textit{developmental interpretability}, which aims to understand models through their evolution across the learning process. More broadly, this work takes a step towards establishing the correspondence between data distributional structure, geometric properties of the loss landscape, learning dynamics, and emergent computational structures in neural networks.

papers.title: Semantic Hierarchical Reinforcement in Large Language Models for Contextual Memory Persistence
papers.research_question: How can semantic hierarchical reinforcement improve contextual memory persistence and coherence in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Semantic Hierarchical Reinforcement, a method that embeds hierarchical semantic structures into LLMs to enhance memory retention and contextual coherence through dynamic reinforcement mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Semantic Hierarchical Reinforcement provides a scalable and effective approach to advance contextual memory in LLMs, improving coherence and retention across diverse applications.
papers.key_findings:
Substantial improvements in contextual coherence, memory retention rates, and task-specific accuracy compared to baseline models.
The method scales effectively with dataset size, maintaining performance on large datasets without significant degradation.
Demonstrates robustness under noisy input conditions, with better resilience in contextual coherence.
Optimal performance is achieved at intermediate hierarchical depths, balancing complexity and computational efficiency.
Exhibits slower memory decay over time, indicating enhanced long-term retention capabilities.
papers.limitation:
Excessive depth in semantic hierarchies introduces diminishing returns due to computational overhead.
Computational demands increase significantly with larger models, affecting scalability.
Effectiveness depends heavily on the quality and structure of input data, limiting generalization in domain-specific tasks.
future_direction: Explore more efficient algorithms for hierarchical construction and reinforcement to reduce resource intensity.
Integrate distributed computing frameworks to alleviate scalability constraints.
Develop adaptive pre-processing pipelines to tailor hierarchical structures to specific task demands.
papers.abstract: This study introduces a hierarchical semantic structure within memory layers of large language models, the methodology facilitates dynamic prioritization of contextually significant information, enabling improved alignment between abstract concepts and task-specific details. Iterative clustering algorithms and adaptive reinforcement layers provide the foundation for scalable integration of structured memory mechanisms, balancing computational efficiency with performance gains. Experimental evaluations demonstrate substantial improvements in memory retention rates, contextual coherence, and task accuracy, particularly in scenarios involving extended sequences and complex multi-turn interactions. The robustness of the approach was evident under varying noise levels and input conditions, showing its adaptability across a wide spectrum of tasks. Comparative analysis highlighted consistent advantages over baseline methodologies, with the proposed model achieving superior semantic alignment and efficiency metrics. Hierarchical depth was shown to influence performance outcomes, revealing an optimal balance between complexity and scalability. Furthermore, memory retention analyses indicated a slower rate of decay, reinforcing the efficacy of semantic reinforcement in preserving relevant contextual details over time. The framework also demonstrated practical scalability across larger datasets, maintaining its effectiveness without significant degradation. Collectively, the findings establish a robust paradigm for addressing foundational challenges in contextual memory frameworks for advanced language models.

papers.title: Structural analysis of an all-purpose question answering model
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in a multi-task question answering model specialize for different tasks, and why does the model retain single-task performance despite limited transfer effects?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an all-purpose question answering model that retains single-task performance, and through attention head masking analysis, shows that heads specialize by task and some are more conducive to learning.
papers.conclusion: The all-purpose model can answer both boolean and extractive questions without significant performance drop, and attention head analysis reveals specialization and learning-prone heads.
papers.key_findings:
The all-purpose question answering model retains single-task performance despite limited transfer between boolean and extractive tasks.
Attention head importance is highly task-dependent, with heads specializing in specific tasks; for example, the most important head for SQuAD is the least important for BoolQ.
Some attention heads are more conducive to learning across both single-task and multi-task settings, reminiscent of the lottery ticket hypothesis.
Masking specific heads can recover or even improve single-task performance, indicating task specialization.
Intermediate layers have a stronger effect on model performance when heads are masked compared to other layers.
papers.limitation:
The head importance scoring method does not account for interactions between heads.
Fine-tuning is a brittle process, and results should be averaged over multiple runs.
future_direction: Conduct structural analysis on new tasks or a greater number of tasks at once.
Investigate other head importance metrics that take into account interactions between heads.
papers.abstract: Attention is a key component of the now ubiquitous pre-trained language models. By learning to focus on relevant pieces of information, these Transformer-based architectures have proven capable of tackling several tasks at once and sometimes even surpass their single-task counterparts. To better understand this phenomenon, we conduct a structural analysis of a new all-purpose question answering model that we introduce. Surprisingly, this model retains single-task performance even in the absence of a strong transfer effect between tasks. Through attention head importance scoring, we observe that attention heads specialize in a particular task and that some heads are more conducive to learning than others in both the multi-task and single-task settings.

papers.title: Pre-training Limited Memory Language Models with Internal and External Knowledge
papers.research_question: Can factual memorization be disentangled from language understanding in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Limited Memory Language Models (LMLM), a pre-training method that externalizes factual knowledge to an external database, disentangling knowledge from language understanding and enabling editable and verifiable knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LMLMs offer a pathway toward language models with substantially reduced dependency on parameter count for factual accuracy and enable precise control over factual knowledge through an external database.
papers.key_findings:
LMLMs achieve lower perplexity than standard models of the same size during pre-training.
LMLMs improve factual precision over standard models and approach the performance of much larger models.
LMLMs support instant unlearning by simply removing database entries, without degrading model utility.
LMLMs learn to generate lookup calls effectively and rely on the external database for facts.
LMLMs do not compromise general language understanding capabilities, as shown by NLU benchmark performance.
papers.limitation:
Incur upfront costs for data annotation and model training.
Currently focuses on entity-level atomic facts; extending to more complex knowledge structures is future work.
future_direction: Extend LMLM to more complex knowledge structures beyond entity-level facts.
Integrate LMLM with symbolic reasoning and knowledge representation.
Scale LMLM to larger models and databases.
papers.abstract: Neural language models are black-boxes--both linguistic patterns and factual knowledge are distributed across billions of opaque parameters. This entangled encoding makes it difficult to reliably inspect, verify, or update specific facts. We introduce Limited Memory Language Models (LMLM), a new class of language models that externalizes factual knowledge to external database during pre-training rather than memorizing them. Our pre-training approach strategically masks externally retrieved factual values from the training loss, thereby teaching the model to perform targeted lookups rather than relying on memorization in model weights. Our experiments demonstrate that LMLMs achieve competitive performance compared to significantly larger LLMs on standard benchmarks, while offering the advantages of explicit, editable, and verifiable knowledge bases.

papers.title: Trained recurrent neural networks develop phase-locked limit cycles in a working memory task
papers.research_question: What kind of neural dynamics support phase coding of information with neural oscillations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that phase-coded memories in working memory correspond to limit cycle attractors arising from the coupling of internal oscillations to an external reference oscillation.
papers.conclusion: The study suggests that neural networks can implement phase coding for working memory through multi-stable coupling of internal and external oscillations.
papers.key_findings:
Trained RNNs develop phase-locked limit cycles when performing a working memory task.
Phase-coded memories correspond to separate limit cycle attractors in the dynamical landscape.
The stability of these attractors depends on the amplitude and frequency of the reference oscillation.
The networks can be described as two phase-coupled oscillators, with one generating an oscillation and the other implementing a coupling function.
A reduced model with functional modules captures the essential dynamics.
papers.abstract: Neural oscillations are ubiquitously observed in many brain areas. One proposed functional role of these oscillations is that they serve as an internal clock, or 'frame of reference'. Information can be encoded by the timing of neural activity relative to the phase of such oscillations. In line with this hypothesis, there have been multiple empirical observations of such phase codes in the brain. Here we ask: What kind of neural dynamics support phase coding of information with neural oscillations? We tackled this question by analyzing recurrent neural networks (RNNs) that were trained on a working memory task. The networks were given access to an external reference oscillation and tasked to produce an oscillation, such that the phase difference between the reference and output oscillation maintains the identity of transient stimuli. We found that networks converged to stable oscillatory dynamics. Reverse engineering these networks revealed that each phase-coded memory corresponds to a separate limit cycle attractor. We characterized how the stability of the attractor dynamics depends on both reference oscillation amplitude and frequency, properties that can be experimentally observed. To understand the connectivity structures that underlie these dynamics, we showed that trained networks can be described as two phase-coupled oscillators. Using this insight, we condensed our trained networks to a reduced model consisting of two functional modules: One that generates an oscillation and one that implements a coupling function between the internal oscillation and external reference. In summary, by reverse engineering the dynamics and connectivity of trained RNNs, we propose a mechanism by which neural networks can harness reference oscillations for working memory. Specifically, we propose that a phase-coding network generates autonomous oscillations which it couples to an external reference oscillation in a multi-stable fashion.

papers.title: Interpret, prune and distill Donut : towards lightweight VLMs for VQA on document
papers.research_question: How can we compress large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) while preserving task accuracy? Can mechanistic interpretability help address this limitation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a model compression method (Donut-MINT) that uses mechanistic interpretability to guide pruning and knowledge distillation, yielding a lightweight VLM that maintains strong performance on document VQA.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability can effectively guide pruning and architectural simplification for VLMs, resulting in compact models (Donut-MINT) that maintain high accuracy on document VQA while reducing computational cost.
papers.key_findings:
The final cross-attention layer (C3) and specific heads within it are critical for transcribing text from image patches.
The feed-forward layer M3 acts as a cleaner for the residual stream from C3 and can be removed.
Early decoder layers (S0, C0, M0) transform token embeddings, with M0 mapping tokens to lowercase representations, allowing for layer pruning via token reprojection.
For keyword-based questions, self-attention layers propagate information from the keyword to the answer token, forming a semantic query.
For contextualized questions in structured documents, the model uses positional information from keys to retrieve corresponding values, requiring at least two cross-attention layers.
papers.limitation:
The utility of pruned attention heads may be task or domain dependent; they are not universally redundant.
The current pipeline relies on manual inspection and bespoke tools, limiting scalability.
Knowledge distillation uses only final logits, not intermediate activations that are now better understood.
future_direction: Incorporate intermediate activations into distillation via auxiliary losses.
Automate interpretability-driven pruning to scale to larger models and diverse architectures.
Develop adaptive corruption techniques and automated circuit discovery for VrDU.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Visually-rich Document Understanding rely on large Vision-Language Models like Donut, which perform document-level Visual Question Answering without Optical Character Recognition. Despite their effectiveness, these models are too costly for real-time or resource-constrained applications. We investigate model compression through knowledge distillation, training compact student models from a larger teacher. We leverage mechanistic interpretability to drive student architecture design within this framework. By analyzing internal computations, we identify essential subcomponents to retain, while having a clear view of which subcomponents should be approximated, skipped, or reparametrized based on their function.
